sessions.title: From Python scripts to explicit contracts
sessions.outcome: use Cargo, types, functions, expressions, and slices to summarize telemetry. Allow eight hours including the first exercise.
sessions.html:
Outcome: use Cargo, types, functions, expressions, and slices to summarize telemetry. Allow eight hours including the first exercise.

In a Python pipeline, assumptions about a value may live in conventions and runtime checks. Rust asks you to state more of those assumptions in types. A duration represented as u64 cannot be negative, but its type alone does not tell you whether the unit is milliseconds or seconds. Naming and domain wrappers still matter.

let creates an immutable binding by default; let mut permits mutation. Shadowing introduces a new binding and can change its type. Blocks evaluate to their final expression when it has no trailing semicolon. An if can therefore produce a value.

Complete program:

fn classify(latency_ms: u64) -> &'static str {
    if latency_ms > 500 { "slow" } else { "normal" }
}

fn main() {
    let latencies = [120_u64, 800, 240];
    for latency in latencies {
        println!("{latency}: {}", classify(latency));
    }
}

&'static str is suitable here because both results are string literals stored for the program's duration. It would not be suitable for returning a reference to a newly constructed local String.

A slice such as &[u64] lets a function inspect a contiguous sequence without owning its storage. It accepts borrowed arrays and vectors. For an empty sequence, an average is undefined; Option<f64> makes the caller handle that case. Returning zero would confuse no observations with observed zero latency.

Walkthrough: design mean_latency(&[u64]) -> Option<f64>. Check emptiness first. Convert values before summing to avoid overflowing an integer accumulator. Floating-point conversion sacrifices exactness for very large integers, so define the result as an approximate mean. Do not promise exact accounting with this representation.

Practice: implement exercise 01. Then add a maximum-latency function and a slow-request counter with a configurable threshold. Predict boundary results before running.

Checkpoint: Why is None preferable to 0.0 for empty input? What changes when a semicolon is added to a function's final expression? Does a borrowed slice require a new allocation?

Read: Rust Book: common programming concepts; Rustlings variables, functions, primitive types, and control flow.

Workshop: Make telemetry assumptions executable

Observable goals

  • Write a function accepting both borrowed arrays and vectors through a slice.
  • Specify empty-input behavior and units before implementing statistics.
  • Explain a compiler type error using the expected and actual types.

Predict and inspect

For latencies [0, 500, 501] and the rule latency > 500, predict the slow count and mean. Now predict the result for an empty input. Which answer represents missing observations without inventing a measurement?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

The count is 1; the approximate mean is 1001.0 / 3.0. A function returning Option<f64> can distinguish None from Some(0.0). Converting each u64 before summation avoids integer-sum overflow, but does not provide exact arithmetic for all large integers. Write that limitation in your contract. In Python, an empty NumPy reduction may produce a warning or NaN; here the return type makes the choice visible to callers.

AI collaboration: ask AI to scaffold the summary struct and CLI. Inspect units and error paths before accepting the diff.

Guided practice

  1. Reproduce: implement mean, maximum, and threshold count; test the three-element input above.
  2. Change: accept a threshold argument and test equality at 500. Run the same functions on an array and a vector.
  3. Transfer: design a LatencyMs wrapper and explain which mistakes it prevents and which values still require validation.
Hint — start with the contract

Return early on an empty slice. Maximum naturally returns an Option too. A domain wrapper distinguishes milliseconds from token counts; it does not prove the sensor measured correctly.

Work in practice/src/lib.rs. Run one named exercise suite at a time. The reference implementation is in practice/src/solutions.rs.

Exercise 01: latency summary

Implement mean_latency(values: &[u64]) -> Option<f64>.

  • Empty input returns None.
  • Values are nonnegative milliseconds; nonempty input returns an approximate arithmetic mean.
  • Do not overflow a u64 sum for large inputs.
  • Do not mutate or copy the input into a new collection.

Examples: [] -> None; [100, 200, 300] -> Some(200.0); [0] -> Some(0.0).

Stretch: implement p95 with an explicitly chosen definition. For nearest-rank p95 on a nonempty sorted sample of n values, use rank ceil(0.95*n) with one-based indexing. Explain why a streaming exact percentile has different memory requirements from a streaming mean.

Exercise 02: borrowed prompt selection

Implement first_nonempty(values: &[String]) -> Option<&str>.

  • Inspect entries in order and trim surrounding whitespace using Rust's str::trim semantics.
  • Return a borrowed view of the first nonempty result.
  • Return None when all entries are blank or input is empty.
  • Do not allocate an output string or mutate the source.

Example: [" ", " retrieve ", "answer"] -> Some("retrieve").

Stretch: draw owner/reference lifetimes and show an intentionally noncompiling attempt to return a reference into a local String.

Exercise 03: validated token budget

Implement validate_budget(requested: u64, limit: u64) -> Result<(), BudgetError>.

  • A zero limit always yields ZeroLimit, even when requested is zero.
  • Otherwise requested above limit yields Exceeded { requested, limit }.
  • Equality and zero requested with positive limit are valid.

sessions.title: Ownership as a resource contract
sessions.outcome: distinguish moving, borrowing, and cloning; choose appropriate string types.
sessions.html:
Outcome: distinguish moving, borrowing, and cloning; choose appropriate string types.

A String owns a growable UTF-8 allocation. Assignment normally transfers its ownership. This is different from assigning a Python name to an existing object. After a move, the old Rust binding cannot be used as though it still owns the value.

Intentionally failing fragment:

let prompt = String::from("summarize this report");
let queued_prompt = prompt;
println!("{prompt}"); // use after move

There are several valid repairs with different meanings. Use &prompt if the receiver only needs temporary access. Move the string if the receiver should own it. Use prompt.clone() when independent ownership and the allocation/copy cost are intentional. Automatically cloning every compiler complaint hides architectural decisions.

&str is a borrowed UTF-8 view. &String borrows a particular container; &str accepts a broader class of text, including slices and literals. Prefer fn inspect(prompt: &str) for read-only text. Use String when storing or transferring ownership of text. A borrow prevents the owner from being dropped while that reference is used.

Complete program:

fn label(prompt: &str) -> &str {
    prompt.trim()
}

fn main() {
    let prompt = String::from("  summarize  ");
    let cleaned = label(&prompt);
    println!("{cleaned}");
    println!("original: {prompt}");
}

trim() returns a view into the original text. The returned borrow cannot outlive the original String. UTF-8 also means byte offsets are not necessarily character boundaries; arbitrary byte slicing may panic. A future document chunker must explicitly define byte, character, or tokenizer-based boundaries.

Multiple shared references can coexist. An exclusive mutable reference excludes other conflicting accesses while it is active. The compiler often ends a borrow at its last use, rather than at the end of its enclosing block.

Practice: implement exercise 02 without allocating output. Draw which allocation each reference points to. For Lab A, compare passing a whole log record by value against borrowing it for statistics.

Checkpoint: Does move always copy heap bytes? Why can returning local_string.as_str() fail? When is a clone a sensible design?

Read: Rust Book ownership; Brown ownership; Rustlings move semantics and strings.

Workshop: Trace owners before repairing code

Observable goals

  • Identify the owner and final use of each borrow in a short program.
  • Repair a borrow conflict without an unnecessary clone.
  • Distinguish UTF-8 byte length from a token or character count.

Predict and inspect

let mut prompt = String::from("  agent  ");
let view = prompt.trim();
prompt.clear();
println!("{view}");

Predict whether this compiles. Mark the allocation, the owner, and the last use of view before asking the compiler.

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

view refers into prompt and is used after clear, so mutation conflicts with the active shared borrow. Printing view before clearing removes that overlap. Creating an owned copy also works, but has a different allocation contract. A lifetime annotation cannot make the conflicting accesses safe. Use the compiler's span information to compare your predicted last use with the actual one.

sessions.title: Model agent state and failure explicitly
sessions.outcome: use structs for product types, enums for alternatives, and Result for expected failures.
sessions.html:
Outcome: use structs for product types, enums for alternatives, and Result for expected failures.

An agent execution can be pending, running, succeeded, or failed. Representing it with several independent booleans permits contradictory states. An enum restricts the available shapes:

enum Execution {
    Pending,
    Running { attempt: u32 },
    Succeeded { output: String },
    Failed { message: String, retryable: bool },
}

This prevents some invalid combinations but does not enforce a legal transition history. A transition function must still reject success-to-running or retry after a nonretryable failure.

Option<T> means a value may be absent. Result<T, E> means an operation succeeds or returns a classified error. Use match when branches need different policies. The ? operator returns early on error, converting compatible errors when needed; it does not decide whether retry is safe.

Worked design: a token request is valid when the configured limit is positive and requested tokens do not exceed it. Make zero-limit configuration failure distinct from an oversized request. Validate configuration first so (0, 0) has an unambiguous outcome. Exercise 03 encodes this contract.

Borrowing interacts with pattern matching. Matching an owned enum may move its fields. Matching &execution inspects without consuming it. Select based on whether the caller needs the state afterward.

For a server, malformed requests and upstream outages are normal failure paths, not reasons to panic. unwrap() can be reasonable in a test that establishes its precondition, but request handlers should propagate and classify errors. Never equate memory safety with correct retry or business semantics.

Practice: implement exercise 03, then add advance(state, event) -> Result<Execution, TransitionError>. Test illegal transitions. Finish Lab A with explicit invalid-row counts.

Checkpoint: What can the enum prevent? What requires runtime validation? Why should a timeout not automatically mean a side-effecting operation did nothing?

Read: Rust Book enums, pattern matching, and error handling; Rustlings options and errors.

Workshop: Test domain invariants at construction

Observable goals

  • Represent agent execution alternatives without contradictory flags.
  • Propagate an expected error through Result rather than panicking.
  • Check a token-budget calculation without overflow.

Predict and inspect

A request has a context limit of 8,192, a prompt of 8,000, and reserves 256 output tokens. Is it valid? What if prompt plus reserve exceeds the integer type's range before comparison?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

The total 8,256 exceeds the limit by 64. checked_add distinguishes arithmetic overflow from an ordinary over-budget result. Use a constructor returning a domain error so callers cannot accidentally construct a validated request through public fields. An enum such as Execution::Failed { reason } couples the failure state to its explanation. Result does not automatically enforce valid transitions; transition methods still need rules.

sessions.title: Retrieval APIs, lifetimes, traits, and iterators
sessions.outcome: build a small retrieval core without unnecessary text copies.
sessions.html:
Outcome: build a small retrieval core without unnecessary text copies.

Lifetime annotations describe relationships between references; they do not keep allocations alive or extend their lifetime. If a function returns a selected document borrowed from its input collection, the result must remain tied to that collection.

struct Document {
    id: String,
    text: String,
}

fn find_document<'a>(docs: &'a [Document], id: &str) -> Option<&'a Document> {
    docs.iter().find(|doc| doc.id == id)
}

The result borrows from docs, not from id. This distinction matters when there are multiple input references. In simple one-reference functions, lifetime elision often expresses the relationship without written annotations.

iter() borrows elements; iter_mut() borrows them exclusively; into_iter() consumes a collection when called on an owned vector. An iterator pipeline is lazy until consumed. collect() materializes a result and can allocate. Replacing a loop with iterator syntax alone does not prove a speedup.

A trait defines shared behavior. For Lab B, start with trait Scorer { fn score(&self, query: &str, doc: &Document) -> f64; }. Use a generic function for a known scorer type. Investigate &dyn Scorer only when runtime substitution is actually needed. Dynamic dispatch and static dispatch are different tools, not a beginner ranking of good and bad.

Separate a pure ranking function from file loading and network calls. This makes edge cases cheap to test. Define deterministic ordering for equal scores and a policy for nonfinite values before using sorting APIs.

Practice: Lab B. Add a scorer that uses simple token overlap; it is an educational baseline, not a claim of semantic retrieval quality. Return references to documents and store only score/index metadata during ranking.

Checkpoint: Can annotations make a local temporary safe to return? Which iterator consumes the document collection? What must change if results need to outlive that collection?

Read: Rust Book generics/traits/lifetimes, closures/iterators, and modules. Use Comprehensive Rust as a concise second explanation.

Workshop: Make retrieval ownership and ranking precise

Observable goals

  • Explain a returned reference's relationship to its input lifetime.
  • Implement a deterministic scalar similarity reference.
  • State a policy for dimension mismatch, zero norms, and non-finite values.

Predict and inspect

Would fn best<'a>(items: &'a [Document]) -> Option<&'a Document> keep documents alive after their owner is dropped? Does a lifetime annotation allocate or extend storage?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

The annotation describes a relationship checked at compile time; it does not retain the owner. For a similarity calculation, zip alone silently stops at the shorter input. Check equal dimensions before accumulation. For equal scores, choose a stable document-ID tie rule so two valid implementations have comparable outputs. Decide whether zero vectors produce a domain error or a documented special score before optimizing.

sessions.outcome: process JSONL records incrementally and report actionable errors.
sessions.html:
Outcome: process JSONL records incrementally and report actionable errors.

Deserializing a record gives you a structural type; it does not validate all business rules. A string ID may still be empty, a duration may use the wrong unit, and duplicated IDs may violate your downstream contract. Keep parsing and validation separate so errors identify the failed stage.

Use Serde for typed records and serde_json for JSON. With BufRead, read a line, enforce a size policy, parse it, validate it, update a summary or send it downstream, then release its storage. Loading the entire file into a vector defeats the bounded-memory objective.

Memory is not automatically bounded merely because you iterate over lines. A single enormous line can grow a buffer; a deduplication set grows with unique IDs; retaining error messages grows with error count. Lab C therefore requires a line-size limit and capped error samples. If the input is untrusted, enforce the byte cap while reading rather than only checking after an unbounded read_line.

Store no source text in routine error logs. Decide whether unknown JSON fields are acceptable; schema evolution and strictness have different costs.

For chunking, start with Unicode character boundaries. A character count is not a token count, so name the parameter accordingly. Later, a model-specific tokenizer can replace it behind a clear interface.

sessions.title: CPU concurrency and shared ownership
sessions.outcome: distinguish work parallelism, shared ownership, and synchronized mutation.
sessions.html:
Outcome: distinguish work parallelism, shared ownership, and synchronized mutation.

Threads can execute CPU work in parallel. Ownership transfer into a thread prevents the parent from casually reusing transferred data. Shared immutable data can use Arc<T>, an atomically reference-counted owner. Cloning an Arc clones a handle and increments its count; it does not deeply clone T. Arc alone does not make arbitrary mutation safe.

Use Mutex<T> when protecting shared mutable state. Hold the lock for the smallest meaningful operation. A common ingestion design gives each worker its own partial statistics, then combines results; this can avoid a global lock for each record.

Worked design: one reader produces bounded batches, a fixed number of workers transforms them, and an aggregator merges summaries. If output order matters, attach sequence numbers and explicitly bound the reorder buffer. An unbounded reorder buffer can eliminate the memory advantage of a bounded input queue.

Measure first with one worker. More threads may lose to serialization, I/O, allocation overhead, or memory bandwidth. Native Python numerical libraries may already use optimized multithreaded kernels, so compare against the actual baseline, not a deliberately slow substitute.

CPU work should not occupy an async executor thread for long periods. Later, use an appropriate bounded CPU pool or blocking bridge. A blocking bridge also needs a concurrency policy; moving unlimited work to it does not solve overload.

Practice: extend Lab C with a fixed worker count. Keep output equal to the serial version. Test a worker failure without silently losing a batch. Write down whether your ordering and failure requirements justify the complexity.

Two threads each load an atomic counter, add one locally, and store the result. Can the final count be one even if every operation uses sequential consistency?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

Both threads may load zero before either store. Strong ordering does not turn a multi-operation sequence into one indivisible update. An atomic read-modify-write such as fetch_add addresses this particular counter; a multi-field invariant may need a lock or another design. Likewise, Arc<T> shares ownership but does not make arbitrary T mutations safe. Prefer worker-local results merged at a clear boundary when possible.

sessions.outcome: explain futures and task ownership, and run independent I/O concurrently.
sessions.html:
Outcome: explain futures and task ownership, and run independent I/O concurrently.

An async function creates a future describing work. That future needs polling to make progress. Calling an async function without awaiting or scheduling it does not mean the operation has completed. Awaiting two independent operations sequentially can leave concurrency unused.

Tokio schedules tasks that should yield while waiting for I/O. This is useful for many network requests; it does not automatically accelerate a CPU-heavy tokenizer. A task spawned with Tokio typically requires owned or otherwise suitably long-lived data. The 'static requirement does not mean a task must run forever; it means its captured data cannot contain unsuitable short-lived references.

// Illustrative fragment inside a Tokio async context.
let endpoint = String::from("local-mock");
let handle = tokio::spawn(async move {
    tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(20)).await;
    endpoint.len()
});
let length = handle.await?;

async move transfers captures into the future. Awaiting a JoinHandle can reveal task failure separately from the operation's own returned error. If a task returns Result, distinguish both layers. Dropping a JoinHandle generally detaches the task; it is not a reliable cancellation policy.

Walkthrough: create ten synthetic tool calls with varied delays. Start with serial execution, then a bounded concurrent executor. Record start/end times and output IDs. Decide whether results are returned in input order or completion order.

Practice: Lab D phase one. Use synthetic sleeps and errors so no API keys or network variability are involved. Read the Mini-Redis shared-state and channels code as examples of ownership boundaries.

A blocking-task facility moves execution, but unrestricted submissions can simply move the resource problem to another queue. Establish a concurrency bound, and remember that already-running blocking work generally cannot be stopped by dropping its awaiting future.

sessions.html:
Outcome: enforce resource limits and define failure behavior.

A semaphore bounds active operations. It does not by itself bound queued callers, allocated task objects, request bodies, or waiting time. A robust executor defines admission capacity, active capacity, queue capacity, queue timeout, and end-to-end deadline separately.

Walkthrough: choose four active jobs and eight queued jobs. Admit jobs through a bounded channel. Reject when full according to a documented policy. Each admitted job carries an absolute deadline that includes queue time. Before starting work, calculate the remaining budget; expired jobs must not consume an upstream attempt.

Acquire capacity before starting expensive work, and keep the permit owned by the scope that performs it. Ensure the permit drops on success, error, cancellation, and panic unwind. Tests should observe available capacity after every path, rather than merely checking returned error strings.

Cancellation is cooperative and operation-specific. Dropping a future may stop local polling but cannot undo a request already accepted by a remote tool. A timeout around a JoinHandle also does not automatically stop its underlying task. Retain control over spawned tasks, abort where appropriate, and await their termination; account for blocking work that cannot be interrupted that way.

Retries need a classified error, attempt bound, remaining time budget, and side-effect policy. Never retry an unsafe side effect merely because a timeout occurred. Even an inference retry after streaming begins can duplicate or contradict output. This course disables retries once response bytes have been sent.

Practice: Lab D phase two. Make the clock controllable in tests. Add queue expiry, caller cancellation, and an upstream that never completes. Show that the service accepts new work afterward.

A framed protocol can retain partial bytes in an owned buffer across waits. A deadline should include queue delay: a 100 ms budget with 80 ms already queued leaves roughly 20 ms, not another fresh 100 ms per retry. Remote side effects require protocol-level idempotency or reconciliation.

Outcome: implement a narrow, explicit gateway contract with Axum.

Your FastAPI experience transfers to routes, request validation, dependency/state injection, and HTTP semantics. Rust adds compile-time type and ownership constraints around those boundaries. Keep handlers thin: decode, validate, invoke application logic, then map the result to a response.

For the learning gateway, define a small local API rather than claiming full compatibility with an existing inference API. POST /generate accepts a model name, prompt, and output-token budget. Validate body size and budget before acquiring scarce upstream capacity. Use one reusable outbound HTTP client so connection pooling can work across requests.

Application state may own shared configuration, the client, and concurrency controls through Arc or cloneable handles. Mutable per-request data belongs to that request. A mutex around the entire upstream call would serialize requests and hold a lock over slow I/O.

Walkthrough: route GET /health/live to process liveness. Route GET /health/ready to admission readiness as defined by your service. A brief queue being full need not imply the process should restart. Document whether readiness includes upstream health and how its check is cached.

Define an error mapping: malformed input 400, invalid semantic values 422, body too large 413, admission overload 429, upstream failure 502, and exhausted deadline 504. These are course design choices; implement and test one consistent contract. Errors should include a stable category and request ID, not raw secrets or provider internals.

sessions.title: Streaming and observable failure
sessions.outcome: forward a stream incrementally and diagnose partial failures.
sessions.html:
Outcome: forward a stream incrementally and diagnose partial failures.

HTTP transport chunks are arbitrary byte fragments. An SSE event or a JSON value may span multiple chunks. A gateway can either transparently forward bytes or parse events using a proper incremental decoder. Do not assume each received chunk is a complete token event.

Once response headers and body bytes have been sent, the server cannot replace them with a fresh 502 response. Decide the wire contract for mid-stream failure: for this course, terminate the stream and emit a correlated failure event to telemetry. If you add application-level SSE error events, specify that extension to clients explicitly.

Hold the upstream concurrency permit until the response body finishes or is dropped, not just until response headers arrive. Otherwise, the number of active generations can exceed the configured limit. A downstream disconnect should release local resources and close the upstream response; this still does not prove remote GPU computation stops immediately.

Trace queue wait, upstream connection/headers, time to first forwarded content, stream completion, and error category separately. A request may succeed at the HTTP status level but fail during its body. Logs should capture this distinction without recording prompts by default.

Walkthrough: use a mock stream split across strange byte boundaries, then a stream that fails after its third event. Verify the client receives initial content before upstream completion. During shutdown, stop admission, give active streams a grace period, and terminate remaining work according to policy.

Practice: Lab E phase two. Measure peak memory for large streams, demonstrate permit recovery on disconnect, and test shutdown with an active request.

Checkpoint: When can HTTP status still change? How long should a permit live? Why is one timestamp insufficient for latency diagnosis?

Read: Axum streaming examples; tracing; Tokio shutdown guidance.

Workshop: Design streaming across arbitrary chunks

Observable goals

  • Distinguish transport chunks from complete application events.
  • Bound buffering for slow clients.
  • Demonstrate a shutdown sequence that accounts for active streams.

Predict and inspect

An SSE event contains an emoji. Can one network chunk end in the middle of its UTF-8 bytes? Can several events arrive in one chunk? What happens if the consumer stops reading?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

Transport boundaries do not define event boundaries. A decoder must retain incomplete bytes and frames until it has a complete valid event. For output, backpressure and disconnect propagation should stop unnecessary production. A shutdown policy needs an admission stop, a grace period, and a defined action when work outlives that period. A final log line is not proof that all producers and consumers terminated.

sessions.title: Rust as a Python component
sessions.outcome: expose a useful native function and measure its complete cost.
sessions.html:
Outcome: expose a useful native function and measure its complete cost.

PyO3 supports Python extension modules written in Rust. Maturin builds and packages them. This enables incremental adoption: retain Python orchestration and move a specific measured operation behind a small interface.

Start with a pure Rust implementation with a precise contract. Then expose a function accepting batches, validate boundary inputs, and map expected failures to Python exceptions. Use the installed PyO3 guide for current module and function syntax. Concurrency and interpreter interaction depend on Python build and PyO3 version; never assume code can access Python objects after releasing interpreter coordination.

Worked design: normalize a batch of document IDs with an ASCII-only rule, preserving order and duplicates. Specify exactly which whitespace and case transformations are allowed. The Python baseline must follow the same rule. A broader Unicode baseline is a different computation and an unfair comparison.

The total runtime includes conversion from Python objects, native work, conversion back, and packaging of results. For small inputs the boundary can dominate. Prefer batch APIs where appropriate. If using numerical arrays later, study ownership, strides, dtype validation, and copy behavior rather than assuming zero-copy interoperability.

Measure tiny, medium, and large batches. Report median and tail measurements over repeated runs, correctness parity, and peak memory. A slower result is useful evidence: you may need a different boundary or should retain the Python implementation.

Practice: Lab F. Build in release mode, record wheel/toolchain versions, and demonstrate a clean virtual-environment install.

Checkpoint: Why can a faster inner function produce a slower Python API? What does batching change? What responsibilities remain at the language boundary?

Read: PyO3 guide, Maturin guide.

Workshop: Choose a Python boundary deliberately

Observable goals

  • Package a small extension with repeatable build instructions.
  • Translate domain errors into appropriate Python exceptions.
  • Measure call, conversion, compute, and return costs separately.

Predict and inspect

A Rust kernel takes 2 microseconds per item, but each Python call adds 10 microseconds of boundary work. What is the approximate single-item cost? What changes if one call processes 100 items and has the same fixed overhead?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

The simplified costs are 12 microseconds for one item and 210 for a batch of 100, or 2.1 per item. This calculation assumes fixed overhead and unchanged compute cost; it is a hypothesis to test, not a benchmark result. Python attachment and safe access to Python objects are API- and version-dependent. Keep Python object access outside detached numerical work, and never assume releasing interpreter attachment makes shared mutable buffers safe.
sessions.lab:
Your learning route

Study and repair: read a small PyO3 example and trace input conversion, native computation, error mapping, and return ownership. Diagnose a benchmark that excludes conversion costs.

Focused reasoning probe: state the boundary contract and draw the cost model. Explain where Python object access must occur for your pinned library version.

AI collaboration: use AI for maturin scaffolding, bindings, and packaging. Inspect generated version-specific API calls and compare scalar/batch outputs with Python.

Review artifact: reproducible wheel/import steps, boundary tests, cost breakdown, and a changed-output-shape adaptation. No unaided package setup is required.

Guided practice

  1. Reproduce: expose one validated scalar function and test it from Python.
  2. Change: add a batch function and compare equivalent outputs with the Python reference.
  3. Transfer: measure empty-call overhead, conversion-only cost, and end-to-end processing; include wheel build and import instructions for your platform.
Hint — hold the workload constant

Compare the same inputs and amount of useful work. A NumPy reference should use its intended vectorized path rather than an artificially slow Python loop.

Review evidence: Python tests, error mapping, pinned PyO3/maturin versions, and a cost breakdown. Revisit ownership before storing borrowed Python data.

Targeted reading: PyO3 performance guide; maturin user guide. Use documentation matching your pinned release; main may describe unreleased behavior.

Module: 11. Budget: four to six hours.

Operation: normalize a list of IDs. Strip only ASCII spaces from each end, change ASCII A–Z to a–z, preserve internal characters, order, duplicates, and empty strings. Non-ASCII characters remain unchanged. Input elements must be Python strings; reject other values with an exception.

Build: pure Rust core, PyO3 wrapper, and Maturin packaging in a separate package/virtual environment. Implement an identical Python baseline. Use the current official guide for the installed API version.

Acceptance: parity on empty batches, ASCII whitespace distinctions, Unicode, duplicate and invalid inputs; installable wheel; no panic exposed as expected input handling.

Benchmark: batches of 1, 100, 10,000, and 100,000 fixed synthetic IDs. Use warm-ups and at least 20 repeated calls per case; report median and p95 with the percentile convention stated. Measure the complete Python call and pure Rust computation separately. Record whether conversion overhead changes the conclusion. A correct report showing no speedup passes.

Hint: Python's default strip() and Unicode lower() do not implement this deliberately narrow contract; use equivalent ASCII rules.

How do you guarantee equivalent benchmark behavior?
When would you keep the implementation in Python?

sessions.title: Architecture review and measured adoption
sessions.outcome: integrate the gateway and defend the design with evidence.
sessions.html:
Outcome: integrate the gateway and defend the design with evidence.

Bring together typed validation, bounded load, stream ownership, explicit errors, and telemetry. Keep the system small enough that you can explain every queue and task. Rust's type system cannot prove service availability, correct tenant isolation, suitable retry policies, or retrieval quality.

Your capstone is a local learning service that fronts a deterministic mock and optionally an existing local inference endpoint. It is not a replacement model runtime. If remote GPU compute dominates end-to-end latency, lower gateway overhead may barely change user latency; memory and overload behavior may still matter.

Write a short architecture decision record. State the workload, why Rust is being considered, alternatives, measured evidence, and cost of maintaining another language. Explain where Python remains: research loops, model experimentation, or agent orchestration where its libraries are useful.

Benchmark the service at below-capacity, near-capacity, and overload workloads. Record offered, accepted, rejected, successful, failed, and unfinished requests. Compute latency over clearly identified populations; reporting only fast successful requests can conceal overload failures. Show throughput and errors alongside latency.

Practice: complete the capstone brief. Reproduce all failure scenarios before increasing features. Present a five-minute walkthrough using one request from admission to body teardown.

Checkpoint: Which invariants are compile-time enforced? Which are tested? Which remain assumptions? What evidence would make you reject a Rust rewrite?

Read: revisit selected Tokio/Axum sources and your own decision log. No new framework is required to finish.

Workshop: Defend an integrated AI gateway

Observable goals

  • Integrate request validation, admission, deadlines, and streaming.
  • Demonstrate predictable behavior during overload and shutdown.
  • Explain architectural tradeoffs using evidence from a reproducible mock.

Predict and inspect

The backend becomes slow while new requests continue arriving. Which resource reaches its bound first? Which metric would distinguish queue waiting from model execution?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

Draw the request path: parse → validate → admit → queue → execute → stream → release. Assign an owner, a bound, a deadline rule, and an observable event to each stage. A shared permit retained until a stream ends bounds something different from one released after response headers. Decide which resource your permit represents. A deterministic mock makes overload, cancellation, and shutdown reproducible without a paid model API.

Guided practice

  1. Reproduce: finish the capstone's happy path with a fixed-seed mock backend.
  2. Change: inject slow execution, backend failure, client disconnect, and shutdown during work.
  3. Transfer: propose one production extension and identify what your mock cannot validate, such as real provider rate limits or model-specific tokenization.
Hint — review one lifecycle end to end

Pick a single cancelled request and follow every task, permit, queue item, and buffer it owns. Then repeat for successful completion.

Review evidence: architecture diagram, run instructions, failure matrix, representative traces, bounded-resource tests, and a short tradeoff memo. Explain one rejected design. Review Sessions 08–10 without opening your notes first.

Targeted reading: Tokio mini-redis repository for lifecycle design; Axum examples for framework-specific patterns. Do not treat an example server as a complete production specification.

Capstone: a bounded AI service gateway

Problem and scope

An inference endpoint is shared by multiple callers. Unrestricted concurrency creates unpredictable queues and resource consumption. Build a local gateway that validates requests, controls admission, forwards streamed responses, and explains failures through telemetry.

Use synthetic requests and a deterministic mock upstream. Connecting to an existing local inference server is optional and requires adapting its actual request/stream protocol. The deliverable is a learning prototype, not a production certification.

Architecture

Client
  -> HTTP validation and request ID
  -> bounded admission queue with absolute deadline
  -> limited active upstream requests
  -> reusable HTTP client -> mock or local inference server
  <- streamed bytes with body-lifetime capacity ownership
  -> structured completion/failure telemetry

Every queue must have a capacity and every task an owner responsible for shutdown. Preserve one end-to-end deadline across queueing and upstream work. Do not hold a global state lock over network I/O.

Milestones

  1. Contract: copy Lab E's local API into a README; define validation and error mapping. Add fixture requests and expected wire responses.
  2. Core service: route validation, configuration, request IDs, mock upstream, and a shared outbound client. Keep parsing separate from execution policy.
  3. Capacity: bounded queue, active cap, queue expiry, overload rejection, and capacity counters. Demonstrate the limits using controlled barriers.
  4. Streaming: incremental forwarding, fragmented chunks, downstream disconnect, and mid-stream failure. Keep capacity occupied until the body finishes or drops.
  5. Lifecycle: stop admission and drain active work within a configurable grace period. Define the fate of queued and unfinished jobs.
  6. Evidence: correctness suite, repeatable load script, results table, and a two-page architecture decision record.

Required failure demonstrations

Scenario Required observation
Invalid request No upstream request is started
Queue at capacity New request rejected according to API contract
Deadline expires in queue Job never begins upstream work
Upstream stalls before headers Deadline error and recovered capacity
Upstream fails mid-body Stream terminates; final telemetry records failure
Client disconnects Local work/resources released; upstream cancellation limitations documented
Shutdown during a stream No new admission; drain/termination follows configured policy
Worker/task fails Failure visible; service can accept later requests

Load experiment

Use fixed upstream response size/delay, a stated load-generation model, and fixed machine configuration. Test below capacity, near capacity, and sustained overload. Run at least five repetitions per case and retain raw results.

Report offered, admitted, rejected, successful, failed, cancelled, and unfinished counts. Define denominator and timing boundaries. Report throughput, success latency p50/p95, time to first content, queue wait, and peak process memory. Treat rejected/failed work explicitly rather than hiding it from a latency chart. Compare versions only under identical workloads.

No speedup target is required. A credible explanation of the bottleneck is more valuable than a misleading percentage. If comparing FastAPI and Rust, use the same upstream, concurrency policy, streaming behavior, and client workload.

Submission checklist

  • A clean checkout can be set up from documented commands.
  • Tests run without paid APIs, GPU availability, or client data.
  • Configuration, dependency versions, and application lockfile are recorded.
  • Each acceptance scenario has a test or reproducible demonstration.
  • Telemetry distinguishes HTTP response start from stream completion.
  • Decision record covers why Rust, why these boundaries, costs, alternatives, and remaining risks.
  • A five-minute demo follows one request through validation, queue, upstream, and teardown.

Review questions

Where can memory still grow? Who owns the request body, task, permit, and response stream? What remains running after the caller leaves? Which errors can be retried safely? Which facts are guaranteed by types, by tests, or only by assumptions? Which component would you keep in Python, and why?
checkpoints: Which invariants are enforced by types versus tests?
Where can memory or unfinished work still accumulate?
What evidence supports or rejects the Rust boundary?

sessions.title: Profiling, experimental design, and performance budgets
sessions.outcome: locate a real bottleneck and design a reproducible experiment before changing code.
sessions.html:
Outcome: locate a real bottleneck and design a reproducible experiment before changing code.

Performance is a property of a workload and an environment. “Rust is faster” is not an experiment. For a RAG ingestion service, separate parsing, normalization, chunking, serialization, and I/O. Define the objective first: records/second at a memory cap, milliseconds/request at a stated arrival rate, or objective evaluations/second. A faster microkernel can have negligible effect on the full pipeline.

Amdahl's law helps bound expectations. If a component consumes 30% of total execution time and becomes twice as fast, ideal total speedup is 1 / (0.7 + 0.3 / 2), about 1.18×, before new overhead. This is a planning model with assumptions, not measured evidence. Use a CPU profile to find hot paths and a timeline to distinguish CPU work from waiting. A wide flamegraph frame indicates sampled stack presence, not a complete diagnosis of why that function is expensive.

Build optimized code with useful symbols. Start with [profile.release] debug = "line-tables-only". sessions.title: Allocation control, borrowing, and buffer reuse
sessions.outcome: reduce allocation pressure while keeping ownership and memory retention explicit.
sessions.html:
Outcome: reduce allocation pressure while keeping ownership and memory retention explicit.

An allocation profile can reveal more than a hot clone() call. A pipeline might allocate for deserialization, normalized text, temporary token lists, output formatting, and queues. Count bytes and lifetimes as well as allocation count. One large retained buffer can matter more than thousands of short-lived tiny objects.

Read-only interfaces should borrow when the owner lives long enough. Cow<'a, str> can preserve a borrowed value when normalization makes no changes and allocate only when necessary. That benefit depends on input distribution and API boundaries: returning a borrowed field from a reusable input buffer prevents you from mutating that buffer while the borrow remains live. For asynchronous queues, owned records or an explicitly shared backing allocation may be the appropriate tradeoff.

Reuse a String or Vec by clearing it between records; clear() retains capacity. Reuse reduces repeated allocation but can retain an unusually large buffer indefinitely. Define a policy such as keeping ordinary buffers and replacing those above a measured capacity threshold after a large record. reserve() is a request for sufficient capacity, not a guarantee of an exact allocation size. Avoid arbitrary worst-case preallocation per worker when multiplying it by the concurrency limit consumes more memory than expected.

Avoid collecting an iterator if a single pass suffices. Replace repeated string concatenation with writing into a reusable output buffer when the profile supports it. Consider inline containers only after observing real length distributions: larger inline storage increases the size of every containing object, including those with no payload. Interning repeated IDs also needs a bounded lifetime; otherwise the interner becomes an unbounded cache.

Worked design: an ingestion worker owns input and output scratch buffers; it parses a record, computes metadata, emits an owned compact result, and releases borrowed views before the next read. The result queue has a byte budget as well as a record cap. Explain exactly where a copy is retained to decouple producer and consumer lifetimes.

Sources

Performance Book: heap allocations, Cow, Vec.

Workshop: Trade allocations against retention

Observable goals

  • Identify allocation sites and distinguish length from retained capacity.
  • Use borrowed output only while its owner remains valid.
  • Evaluate reuse and Cow using a realistic input distribution.

Predict and inspect

A reusable buffer sees one huge document followed by thousands of tiny documents. Does clear() return its capacity to the allocator? Would shrinking on every item necessarily improve throughput?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

Clearing removes contents while keeping capacity for reuse. This can reduce repeated allocations and also retain a large outlier allocation. A retention policy might cap reusable capacity or replace unusually large buffers after use; test the churn this creates. Cow can avoid owning output on an unchanged path, but changed text still needs owned storage. A borrowed view also ties output lifetime to its source.

sessions.title: Data layout, cache locality, and memory bandwidth
sessions.outcome: choose representations based on the fields a hot computation actually accesses.
sessions.html:
Outcome: choose representations based on the fields a hot computation actually accesses.

A vector of structs is convenient, but a loop that reads only one field may bring unrelated fields into cache. A struct of arrays can improve locality for column-oriented operations. Neither representation wins universally: if each operation needs the full record, separate arrays may create additional memory streams and complicate invariants.

Consider candidate vectors with ID, score, metadata, and text. The score kernel should not chase strings and metadata when it only needs a dense numeric slice. Keep stable IDs or indices that reconnect numeric results to owned documents. Check dimensions at the boundary, then use a flat contiguous representation with a documented row stride. Make overflow checks part of computing rows * dimensions before allocation.

An f32 value is four bytes, so scanning n*d coordinates requires at least 4*n*d input bytes, before query traffic and metadata. Divide required bytes by measured elapsed time to estimate effective bandwidth. Do not compare it uncritically with a vendor's peak specification. Cache-resident and larger-than-cache datasets are different workloads; include both. Reading an entire dataset repeatedly can hide cold-start or storage costs.

False sharing occurs when threads modify separate variables that occupy the same coherence unit. A global counter can also introduce true contention. First try worker-local counters and reduction before adding padding everywhere. Cache-line assumptions and alignment differ across machines. Adding padding increases memory consumption and may hurt other accesses.

Representation affects numerical behavior too. Changing reduction order or precision changes rounding; specify tolerance instead of assuming bitwise identity. Do not use repr(packed) as a shortcut to faster access: unaligned fields require care and a smaller layout may be slower. If external binary layout is required, document that as a separate contract.

Observable goals

The embedding payload alone is 1,000,000 × 768 × 4 bytes, about 3.072 GB in decimal units. This is a traffic model, not a measured bandwidth result: caches, repeated passes, and representation affect actual traffic. Separating embeddings from cold metadata can help a scan, but transposition or packing adds costs and may harm other operations. Keep a plain layout as the oracle.

sessions.title: Parallel CPU pipelines with Rayon
sessions.outcome: improve throughput with controlled parallelism, useful task granularity, and explicit numerical reproducibility.
sessions.html:
Outcome: improve throughput with controlled parallelism, useful task granularity, and explicit numerical reproducibility.

Rayon provides data-parallel iterators and work-stealing execution. Adding par_iter() exposes opportunities for parallelism; it does not remove memory-bandwidth limits, scheduling overhead, or dependencies. Tiny tasks may spend more time scheduling than computing. Larger tasks can improve amortization but increase imbalance when record sizes are skewed.

Divide independent records or candidate blocks into chunks, keep scratch state local to workers, and reduce partial results. A shared mutex around every scored candidate usually defeats this design. For global top-k retrieval, compute local top-k per partition, then merge those bounded results. Every globally top-k candidate must be included in its partition's top-k, assuming the same total ordering and tie rules. This can shrink merge work substantially without changing exact selection semantics.

Control the thread budget across the complete application. Python numerical libraries may have their own native pools, and a Rust extension may create additional workers. Multiple layers of parallelism can oversubscribe cores. Use an explicit pool for the experiment, record its size, and compare one worker through the useful hardware range. A physical core count, logical CPU count, and a container CPU quota are different quantities.

Floating-point reduction order can change between parallel executions. If your contract requires reproducible totals, use fixed partitions and a deterministic merge order or another justified summation strategy; measure its cost. Integer counts still need overflow policy. A panic in one worker must not silently turn into a partial successful result.

Async services require an additional CPU admission limit when invoking these jobs. Rayon is not an inference request queue. Keep CPU work off the async executor and make cancellation semantics explicit: dropping an async wait does not instantly preempt already-running CPU kernels.

Sources

Rayon API, Rayon repository, ThreadPoolBuilder.

Observable goals

  • Keep mutable state local to parallel work where possible.
  • Compare worker counts and task granularity against a scalar reference.
  • Describe numerical changes introduced by reduction order.

Can a parallel floating-point sum differ from a sequential sum without a data race? Why might doubling worker count make a memory-heavy scan slower?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

Floating-point addition is not associative, so a different reduction tree can change rounding. Decide whether your contract requires exact ordering, a tolerance, or a higher-precision reference. Parallel speed depends on useful work per task, synchronization, available bandwidth, and competing thread pools. A Python caller, BLAS, and Rayon can each create workers; total runnable threads matter more than one library's setting.

sessions.title: Vectorization, SIMD dispatch, and numeric correctness
sessions.outcome: evaluate compiler vectorization before introducing target-specific SIMD.
sessions.html:
Outcome: evaluate compiler vectorization before introducing target-specific SIMD.

A straightforward loop over contiguous slices can be optimized by the compiler. Help it by exposing clear bounds and access patterns, then inspect generated code or vectorization diagnostics where your toolchain permits. Fewer source lines or explicit intrinsics do not prove better code generation. Include the runtime dispatch and tail handling in the comparison when they exist in the shipped path.

Start with a scalar reference with explicit precision. For dot products, an f64 accumulator over f32 inputs may be more accurate but differ from an f32 SIMD reduction. Compare equivalent precision where possible; otherwise report both speed and error. Fused multiply-add and reassociation can alter rounding. Record the maximum absolute and relative error on adversarial vectors, not only random positive values. Handle cancellation, zeros, extreme finite magnitudes, and dimension tails.

Runtime CPU-feature detection differs from compiling the whole binary for your own machine. A target-cpu=native result is not evidence that a portable distributed binary will perform or even execute identically elsewhere. Isolate target-specific implementations behind architecture guards and runtime feature checks, retaining a scalar fallback. Never execute an AVX2 implementation simply because your development machine supports it.

As checked on 18 October 2026, std::simd is still marked nightly-only experimental in official documentation. The required lab can use safe scalar/autovectorized code on stable Rust. A portable-SIMD nightly branch is optional and must record the pinned nightly toolchain; do not quietly make the entire course require nightly.

Worked design: validate matching dimensions once, dispatch to an appropriate kernel, process full lanes, then process the remainder. Explain valid alignment assumptions and avoid out-of-bounds reads. An unsafe intrinsic wrapper requires a written safety argument even when performance is excellent.

Sources

std::arch, std::simd status, Rust Reference: target_feature.

Compiler auto-vectorization should be the first investigation. Explicit target instructions require a deployment or runtime-dispatch contract. Portable SIMD's std::simd remains experimental and nightly-only in the documentation checked for this course; it is an optional branch, not a stable-course prerequisite.

sessions.title: Exact top-k, indexing, and RAG retrieval efficiency
sessions.outcome: improve retrieval selection by changing the algorithm before tuning the kernel.
sessions.html:
Outcome: improve retrieval selection by changing the algorithm before tuning the kernel.

Sorting all n candidates costs O(n log n) comparisons, while a bounded heap can select top-k in O(n log k) time and O(k) selection storage. A selection algorithm can partition around rank k, followed by sorting the selected subset. Its complexity and additional costs depend on the chosen implementation. Benchmark the real candidate count and k; a full sort can be competitive for small inputs or large k.

Define a total ordering before coding. For this lab, higher finite scores are better; equal scores prefer lexicographically smaller IDs. Reject duplicate IDs and nonfinite scores. Return results ordered by that rule; zero k returns empty, and k above n returns all. A heap's root must represent the worst retained candidate so a better incoming candidate can replace it. Reversing the wrong comparator is an easy way to get plausible but incorrect results.

Avoid copying document text while selecting. Store indices and scores and resolve selected indices against the original owner. Reuse scratch buffers when repeated queries justify it. Precompute query-independent quantities, such as candidate norms, only if your scoring contract allows it and the update policy maintains consistency.

Exact and approximate retrieval optimize different contracts. An approximate index can trade recall, build time, update cost, and memory for latency. Report recall@k against an exact oracle with explicit tie handling and a held-out query set. A lower latency result is not a fair replacement if retrieval quality changes without being disclosed. Likewise, quantized embeddings change numerical precision and may change ranking.

For RAG, include retrieval-stage boundaries: parsing the query, embedding generation, candidate filtering, scoring, selection, and document materialization. A top-k microbenchmark does not measure LLM latency. Use application traces to decide whether selection is worth further effort.

Define descending finite score followed by ascending ID, for example. Reject non-finite scores if that is your contract; total_cmp provides an ordering but does not decide the domain policy for you. This optimization preserves exact scores; ANN changes the search problem and needs recall evaluation.

sessions.title: Tail latency, batching, and queue optimization
sessions.outcome: improve an AI service's latency distribution without hiding rejected work or violating deadlines.
sessions.html:
Outcome: improve an AI service's latency distribution without hiding rejected work or violating deadlines.

Throughput and latency interact through queues. Little's law relates average work in a stable system to throughput and average time in the system, but does not predict a p99 latency or guarantee stability under overload. A service at high utilization can accumulate a long queue even when its median processing time looks healthy.

Separate admission wait, batch assembly, CPU preprocessing, upstream generation, and downstream streaming. A bounded queue avoids unlimited growth but still needs an explicit overload response. An active-request semaphore counts requests, not their token budgets or memory footprint. Consider weighted admission when requests have meaningfully different costs; evaluate whether large requests can starve behind short ones or monopolize capacity.

Dynamic batching amortizes fixed costs but adds waiting. A batching policy needs a maximum batch size, maximum batch wait, and per-request deadlines. Expired items should not start work merely to fill a batch. A client disconnect must free local capacity correctly; it does not prove that a remote GPU job stopped. For LLM serving, avoid implementing a second incompatible scheduler in front of an inference engine without evidence.

Use an open-loop load generator with a stated offered arrival rate when studying queue buildup. A closed-loop client that waits for a response before sending the next request can reduce offered load during stalls, concealing the latency experienced under fixed arrivals. Record dropped generator work and generator saturation. Report success latency alongside acceptance, rejection, timeout, cancellation, and unfinished counts.

Allocation and synchronization changes can affect tail behavior even when average throughput barely moves. Measure at below-capacity, near-capacity, and overload rates, then test a burst of large requests. Keep response semantics, upstream delay distributions, and deadlines unchanged across versions.

Sources

Tokio tutorial, Tokio semaphore, Tokio shutdown.

Workshop: Measure overload, queueing, and tails honestly

Observable goals

  • Distinguish offered, admitted, completed, rejected, and timed-out requests.
  • Measure end-to-end latency including queue time.
  • Evaluate a batching policy under both light and heavy load.

Predict and inspect

A client sends the next request only after the previous reply. When the server stalls, does this client maintain the same offered arrival rate? Could low completed-request p99 hide many timeouts?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

A response-paced generator reduces its offered rate during a stall. Use a scheduled-arrival workload when testing a fixed offered rate, and report generator lag so client saturation is visible. Define latency start at the scheduled or actual submission time explicitly. Track failures alongside successful latencies. Batch waiting can improve compute efficiency and consume the same deadline budget a request needs for useful execution.

sessions.title: Python–Rust boundary optimization and zero-copy tradeoffs
sessions.outcome: optimize the complete Python-facing operation, including conversion and memory ownership.
sessions.html:
Outcome: optimize the complete Python-facing operation, including conversion and memory ownership.

A native function can spend more time converting inputs than computing. Passing one Python string at a time into Rust pays the language boundary repeatedly. Batch APIs can amortize overhead, but enormous batches increase peak memory and the time before the caller gets a result. Optimize batch size against the caller's latency and memory requirements.

For numeric data, inspect dtype, dimensions, strides, contiguity, alignment, mutability, and ownership. A view into a Python-owned array cannot safely outlive its backing storage. “Zero-copy” at one boundary does not mean the subsequent pipeline avoids allocation or packing. A noncontiguous input may require either stride-aware computation or a documented copy; rejecting it is another legitimate explicit contract.

Keep the Rust kernel independent from Python handles. Validate inputs while using the appropriate interpreter context, acquire or copy suitable native views, then perform work under the installed PyO3 version's supported concurrency rules. Python interpreter coordination and free-threaded builds have version-specific behavior. Do not assume detaching from interpreter coordination permits arbitrary access to Python objects or makes all extension code thread-safe.

Model ownership of outputs explicitly. Returning a newly owned array is often simpler than exposing a view into a reusable scratch buffer. A buffer that is reused before Python finishes reading it can corrupt results or create an unsafe boundary. If an owner object retains the storage, document when it can be mutated and when it is released.

Measure against a realistic NumPy baseline, which may already call optimized native kernels. Record thread counts in both stacks. Compare pure kernel time, conversion time where separable, and the complete call. A Rust loop beating a Python loop does not establish an improvement over a vectorized production implementation.

Sources

PyO3 performance guide, Rust NumPy bindings, Maturin guide.

Workshop: Validate numerical buffers at the language boundary

Observable goals

  • Specify dtype, shape, stride, ownership, and mutation policy.
  • Compare batching with equivalent NumPy work including conversion.
  • Keep detached native computation independent of Python object access.

Predict and inspect

A NumPy matrix is sliced with every other column. Does its logical shape imply contiguous storage? Can you safely reinterpret its data as one contiguous Rust slice?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

Shape describes logical indices; strides describe how those indices reach storage. A strided view may require stride-aware access, an explicit contiguous copy, or a clear rejection. Document which path the API takes. Read-only access through one wrapper does not by itself justify assumptions about every possible external alias; follow the pinned binding library's borrowing and thread-safety guarantees. Keep output ownership explicit when returning arrays to Python.

sessions.title: Code generation, build profiles, and justified unsafe boundaries
sessions.outcome: evaluate compiler settings and low-level changes without sacrificing portability or correctness.
sessions.html:
Outcome: evaluate compiler settings and low-level changes without sacrificing portability or correctness.

Optimization level is one input to code generation, not a monotonic speed knob. Compare release settings against the actual workload. Link-time optimization, codegen units, inlining, target features, and panic strategy can change runtime, binary size, compile time, and deployment assumptions. Keep a small experimental matrix rather than changing every flag at once.

Inspect code size when introducing many generic instantiations. Monomorphization can eliminate dispatch overhead but also produce more machine code. Trait-object dispatch can reduce duplication at the cost of indirect calls and lost optimization opportunities. Profile whether this tradeoff matters in the hot path. Do not replace a clean trait API merely because one microbenchmark contains a virtual call.

Profile-guided optimization needs representative training traffic and a separate evaluation workload. Overfitting a profile to one synthetic input can regress another. Record training inputs, compiler version, profile generation/merge commands, and fallback behavior when profiles are unavailable. A configuration that depends on CPU instructions unavailable on deployment machines is not a valid portable release.

Unsafe code transfers proof obligations to the author; it does not disable all checks or inherently improve speed. Before using unchecked indexing, identify the measured check and try restructuring safe iteration. If an unsafe helper remains justified, keep its interface small and document pointer validity, alignment, initialized length, aliasing, and lifetime requirements. Differential tests, boundary cases, and Miri can detect some errors but do not prove soundness or validate all hardware intrinsics. Running Miri is a separate optional nightly toolchain task.

Worked design: replace a repeated bounds-checked multidimensional lookup with a validated shape and safe row slices. Compare generated code before considering unchecked access. If the safe representation removes the bottleneck, retain it. A rejected unsafe patch with sound reasoning is a successful review outcome.

Sources

Cargo profiles, rustc PGO, Rustonomicon, Miri.

Observable goals

  • Explain target compatibility and build reproducibility.

PGO improves the dataset used to collect its profile. Is that sufficient evidence for production? If Miri passes your tests, have you proved all unsafe executions valid?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

Profile-guided optimization reflects the exercised workload. Keep a separate evaluation workload and report profile-generation and instrumented-build steps. CPU-specific flags can restrict deployment compatibility. Miri can find classes of undefined behavior on executed paths, but passing tests is not a universal proof. Unsafe code still needs invariants covering pointer validity, alignment, bounds, aliasing, initialization, and lifetime as applicable.

sessions.title: Numerical optimization engines and experiment throughput
sessions.outcome: optimize a mathematical solver's time-to-quality, not just its loop execution time.
sessions.html:
Outcome: optimize a mathematical solver's time-to-quality, not just its loop execution time.

Systems optimization and mathematical optimization interact. A faster objective evaluator increases experiments per second, but a different algorithm may need fewer evaluations to reach the same solution quality. For your ML and evolutionary-algorithm background, compare evaluation throughput, convergence, and the complete wall-clock budget together.

Begin with ridge-regularized least squares: f(w) = ||Xw - y||² / (2n) + λ||w||² / 2, for n>0 and λ≥0. Its analytic gradient is Xᵀ(Xw-y)/n + λw. Validate shapes and finite inputs, and use finite-difference gradient checks with a stated step and tolerance on small problems. Avoid silently changing sum versus mean scaling: that changes the learning-rate interpretation.

Write a reference gradient-descent solver with maximum iterations, gradient-norm tolerance, finite-value checks, and explicit termination reasons. Select a stable step policy or backtracking line search; an arbitrary learning rate can diverge. If using a library such as argmin for another solver, adapt the same objective and count evaluations consistently. Different stopping conditions do not define an equal-quality comparison.

Reuse residual and gradient buffers and exploit contiguous access before adding threads. Compare parallel matrix/vector work only at useful sizes. For population-based optimization, independent candidate evaluations can be batched or parallelized. Randomness should be derived from a global seed and stable candidate/iteration IDs rather than task completion order; otherwise changing the thread count changes the experiment itself. Store evaluated IDs and objective values so retries do not create ambiguous accounting.

This capstone has two result axes: seconds to a defined objective/gradient target, and solution quality at a fixed wall-clock/evaluation budget. Report failures to converge, variance across seeds, memory, and objective calls. A more approximate kernel that changes ranking or convergence must disclose that tradeoff. Good performance engineering can conclude that an established numerical library is preferable to maintaining a custom kernel.

Sources

argmin documentation, argmin source and examples, Rayon, ndarray.

Workshop: Compare optimizers by time to a validated target

Observable goals

  • Derive and numerically check a small objective's gradient.
  • Separate iteration throughput from solution quality.
  • Compare sequential and parallel evaluation reproducibly.

Predict and inspect

Optimizer A runs 1,000 iterations per second and reaches the target in 5,000 iterations. B runs 600 per second and reaches it in 1,200. Which reaches the target first, ignoring setup? What if one violates the gradient contract?

Worked reasoning — open after your prediction

The simplified times are 5 and 2 seconds respectively; throughput alone picks the wrong winner. For ridge regression define J(w)=||Xw-y||²/(2n)+λ||w||²/2, so ∇J=Xᵀ(Xw-y)/n+λw. State whether an intercept is regularized. Check a small f64 fixture with central differences (J(w+h e_i)-J(w-h e_i))/(2h) over several sensible step sizes; very small steps can amplify rounding. A correct fast implementation and a correct optimization algorithm are separate obligations.

Use a small NumPy calculation as an oracle and check both objective and gradient. Do not silently change regularization scaling between implementations.

Applied challenge: implement ridge objective and gradient with J=||Xw-y||²/(2n)+λ||w||²/2, explicit shape/finite checks, and a solver with documented stopping and failure reasons. Then optimize one measured component.

Acceptance cases: with X=[[1],[2]], y=[1,2], w=[0], λ=0, objective is 1.25 and gradient is −2.5. At w=[1], λ=1, objective is 0.5 and gradient is 1. Add finite-difference checks, invalid shapes, non-finite detection, iteration cap, and a convergence fixture. Compare time to the same quality target, including setup/boundary costs.

Defend: derive the gradient and distinguish faster evaluations from fewer evaluations or changed accuracy.

Transfer at review: change regularization scaling or exclude an intercept from regularization; rederive before coding. If stuck: validate a one-parameter analytical example before adding matrix storage, parallelism, or solver abstraction.

Your learning route

Study and repair: inspect objective and gradient implementations with mismatched mean/sum regularization scaling. Calculate the one-dimensional fixtures by hand and identify the discrepancy.

Core probe: derive and implement only the tiny objective/gradient pair in a supplied test harness. Docs and compiler are allowed; validate the derivation before requesting generated solver code.

AI collaboration: generate solver scaffolding, buffer reuse, parallel population evaluation, and plotting. You own stopping rules, reference parity, seed policy, and time-to-quality comparisons.

Review artifact: gradient checks, convergence/failure evidence, complete-cost results, and an intercept-regularization variation. A faster loop with a changed objective fails even if AI produced convincing explanations.

Schedule and learning outcomes

Budget: approximately 96 hours, eight per module. At eight hours/week this is 12 weeks; allow up to 16 weeks for revision. Each module: two hours lecture/reference reading, four hours implementation, one hour tests, one hour explanation and review. The schedule is adjustable, not a promise of expertise.

Module Focus Demonstrable outcome Assignment
01 Cargo, expressions, scalar types, functions Compute valid telemetry summaries Practice 01
02 Ownership, moves, borrowing, strings Choose an owned or borrowed API deliberately Practice 02; Lab A begins
03 Structs, enums, Option, Result Represent valid state and classify failures Practice 03; Lab A completes
04 Iterators, lifetimes, traits, modules Build a testable retrieval core Lab B
05 Serialization, file I/O, bounded processing Ingest JSONL with useful diagnostics Lab C
06 Threads, Arc, synchronization, CPU work Explain and implement bounded parallel work Lab C extension
07 Futures, Tokio, task ownership Execute independent I/O operations correctly Lab D, first half
08 Backpressure, cancellation, deadlines Bound load and recover capacity after failure Lab D, second half
09 Axum, HTTP contracts, application state Serve validated requests through a gateway Lab E, first half
10 Streaming, testing, tracing, shutdown Preserve stream semantics and diagnose failures Lab E, second half
11 Python interoperability, benchmarks Measure a native extension end to end Lab F
12 Integration and architecture review Defend a gateway's operational tradeoffs Capstone

Mastery gates

  • After 03: explain moves and borrows, handle missing data without panic, pass the three foundation exercise suites.
  • After 06: process a large generated file with bounded application buffering; justify synchronization and identify where copies occur.
  • After 08: demonstrate overload rejection, deadline expiry, and permit recovery with deterministic mock work.
  • After 10: run a local gateway against a mock inference service; demonstrate disconnect and mid-stream failure behavior.
  • After 12: reproduce correctness tests and a benchmark report, and explain where Python remains the better engineering choice.

If a gate fails, spend the next session fixing the gap rather than adding another library.

Advanced optimization track — sessions 13–22

The core remains 96 hours. The advanced track adds approximately 100 hours, for a total of 22 sessions and 196 hours. At eight hours/week, allow another 13–16 weeks for the advanced material and revision. Follow the advanced lectures and lab contracts and use the performance report template.

Session Focus Evidence of mastery Lab
13 Profiling and experimental design Defensible baseline, bottleneck evidence, controlled experiment G: Performance investigation
14 Allocation and buffer ownership Allocation/retention measurements with correct lifetimes H: Allocation-aware normalizer
15 Cache locality and memory layout Layout comparison and bandwidth reasoning I: Candidate scoring layouts
16 Rayon and CPU parallelism Measured break-even batch size, exact results, bounded resources J: Parallel scoring
17 Vectorization and SIMD Numeric error bounds, tail handling, portable fallback K: Similarity kernel
18 Exact top-k and retrieval Algorithm comparisons against a deterministic oracle L: Selection shootout
19 Async tail latency and batching Open-loop load results including rejected/unfinished work M: Gateway latency budget
20 Python–Rust numeric boundaries End-to-end NumPy comparison with ownership/copy accounting N: Batched scoring
21 Code generation and unsafe review Held-out results, deployment assumptions, safety argument O: Optimization review
22 Numerical optimization engines Time-to-quality, gradient checks, reproducible population evaluation P: Optimizer capstone

Advanced mastery gates

  • After 15: reproduce a baseline and show that a representation change preserves correctness; account for retained memory.
  • After 18: prove exact top-k parity, explain task granularity, and measure numerical error for any changed kernel.
  • After 20: separate boundary overhead from native compute and demonstrate the gateway's overload behavior.
  • After 22: defend an optimization using time-to-quality, reproducibility, deployment compatibility, and maintenance cost. A rejected optimization can pass when the evidence supports rejecting it.

Additional directions after the advanced track

  • Data engineering: Arrow/Parquet, lazy execution, and interoperability with the existing Python analytics stack.
  • Agent infrastructure: durable job state, leases, idempotency storage, and tool adapters; a separate protocol study is required before claiming MCP compliance.
  • Inference internals: tensor libraries, model formats, CPU/GPU boundaries, and profiling; do not assume rewriting a gateway accelerates GPU inference.
  • Video systems: bounded frame queues, buffer ownership, and explicit frame-dropping policies.

These remaining directions are optional specializations; the advanced optimization sessions above are fully included as lectures and lab specifications. Learners implement the labs in their local environment.

Learning design: selective core practice and AI collaboration

Each of the 22 sessions has a route in LEARNING_PATHS.md: study and repair an example, complete a short conceptual or implementation probe, build with AI, then defend evidence and adapt a constraint. Core probes target small functions in sessions 01–04, 08, 18, and 22; project scaffolding and integration can use AI throughout. The existing hours and checkpoint IDs remain unchanged. Mastery means engineering control of the result, including AI-assisted code, rather than unaided authorship of every line.

Use native Windows with the MSVC toolchain for this course, or a consistent Linux environment in WSL if you already use one. Keep a project's toolchain, virtual environment, and terminal on the same side of that boundary.

Install and verify
