  2. For the Windows MSVC target, install the required Visual Studio C++ build tools/linker and Windows SDK through the installer. The Rustup Windows guide explains the ABI choices.
  3. Restart your terminal. Use an editor with rust-analyzer.
  4. Verify:
rustup show
rustc --version
cargo --version
rustup component add rustfmt clippy

Use a current stable compiler supporting edition 2024. Record versions in PROGRESS.md. The course does not install or change your machine's toolchain automatically.

Foundation crate

cd D:\working\projects\rust_learning\practice
cargo check
cargo test exercise_01
cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --features solutions

Starter tests intentionally fail at todo!() until implemented. Format or lint failures should be fixed before submitting your work. Reference-solution tests must pass independently of the starter. Rust execution was not verified during course preparation because no local compiler was discoverable.

Later labs

Lab Dependencies to investigate Purpose

Research and curriculum decisions

Checked on 18 October 2026 using public course pages, official documentation, and upstream GitHub repositories. This is a content-fit review, not an exhaustive ranking or a completion of every course. No star-count ranking, performance claim, or guarantee of maintenance is implied. Assessments in the final column are curriculum judgments.

Resource and primary sources Format and scope Fit and decision
The Rust Book, source Language reference presented as a progressive textbook Core reading. Use chapter topics alongside local labs rather than reading cover to cover first.
Comprehensive Rust, GitHub Google course for existing programmers, fundamentals plus specialist tracks Useful concise explanations and concurrency material. Its classroom format is dense for independent study; expand ownership practice and omit Android, Chromium, and embedded tracks.
Rustlings, GitHub Short code exercises recommended alongside the Rust Book Primary warm-up practice. Select exercises by current topic. Short compiler puzzles alone do not establish service-design competence.
100 Exercises to Learn Rust, GitHub Mainmatter course with incremental exercises and tests; assumes another programming language, not systems experience Strong alternative exercise spine. Use selected ownership/type/concurrency sections if Rustlings feels fragmented. Avoid completing two overlapping exercise tracks by default.
Brown Rust Book, ownership Experimental Rust Book fork with ownership visualizations and quizzes Targeted support for Python-to-Rust mental-model changes. Return to official documentation when checking current APIs.
Rust By Practice Additional practice repository; the older sunface URL redirected to this repository when checked Optional remedial exercises, not another required curriculum. Verify current navigation before selecting exercises.
Tokio tutorial, Mini-Redis Async networking tutorial and educational client/server code Core async track after ownership and error handling. Read shared state, channels, spawning, select, and shutdown. Mini-Redis explicitly serves learning, not production Redis replacement.
Axum docs, GitHub and examples HTTP framework documentation and examples Core implementation reference for HTTP labs. This is not a standalone beginner course.
Zero to Production source, author's book site Companion code for a backend engineering book Optional deeper production track. Learn configuration, integration testing, and operations; the local course uses an AI gateway rather than its newsletter domain. The public repository is companion code, not a claim that the entire book is freely available.
PyO3 guide, GitHub, Maturin guide Python interoperability and packaging guides Applied final track for incremental adoption in existing Python systems. Benchmark language-boundary overhead as well as the Rust function.
Rustup Windows guide Platform setup documentation Setup source for MSVC/linker requirements.

How the research changes this course

The general courses establish language progression; local examples translate it to telemetry, retrieval, tool execution, and serving. Ownership receives two modules because aliasing and lifetime decisions will recur in request handling and shared configuration. Async starts only after a learner can explain who owns each value and how failures propagate.

Rustlings is the default short-exercise track. Mainmatter is an alternative or targeted supplement. The Book is the reference spine, Brown is a conceptual supplement, Tokio is the async course, and Axum/PyO3 are implementation references. This avoids assigning several complete introductory courses at once.

The original 12-week estimate has been expanded to approximately 96 hours with a 12–16 week self-study window. Classroom course durations are not treated as mastery estimates. The schedule is a planning assumption and should change based on checkpoint results.

Attribution and reuse

Local lessons and code are original synthesis; they do not reproduce external exercise sets. Follow upstream licenses when copying their materials. For example, Mainmatter's repository identifies CC BY-NC 4.0, and Comprehensive Rust distinguishes documentation and code licenses. Linking here is not a blanket permission to redistribute their content commercially.

Version policy

Source links generally track current stable documentation. Record the actual compiler and crate versions when starting a lab; commit the application Cargo.lock after resolving dependencies. Do not assume an example from an old article matches a current crate API. The foundational starter uses only the standard library and Rust edition 2024; service and extension dependencies are selected during their labs from the linked official docs.

Advanced optimization sources — added 18 October 2026

The advanced track is original course material guided by these primary sources. These are documentation, examples, and reference books rather than ten additional external courses to complete.

Source Used in Selection rationale
Rust Performance Book, GitHub 13–15, 21 Practical profiling, allocation, layout, and code-generation guidance; tool availability depends on OS.
Criterion guide, API 13 and all experiment reports Repeated microbenchmarking; supplemented locally with process repetitions and end-to-end workload measurements.
Rayon docs, GitHub 16, 22 Data parallelism, pool control, and partition-local aggregation.
std::arch, std::simd 17 Architecture and portable-SIMD boundaries. Official std::simd docs still label it nightly-only experimental when checked; stable scalar/autovectorized code remains the required baseline.
BinaryHeap, slice APIs 18 Exact selection, deterministic ordering, and algorithmic alternatives.
Tokio 19 Async resource ownership and bounded concurrency, extended locally into latency-budget experiments.
PyO3 performance, rust-numpy 20 Boundary conversion, ownership, batching, and version-specific interpreter behavior.
Cargo profiles, rustc PGO, Miri 21 Build configuration, profile-guided optimization, and limited dynamic checking of unsafe code.
argmin docs, GitHub 22 Numerical optimization framework and examples. Local exercises add explicit gradient checks, stopping rules, evaluation accounting, and time-to-quality comparisons.

Optimization has two meanings in this track: performance engineering of systems and mathematical search for good solutions. Session 22 explicitly joins the two. No source is used to promise a speedup, and no nightly-only API is silently required by the core course.

Quality upgrade — 18 October 2026

The 22 sessions now include original workshops in WORKSHOPS.md. Source selection favors language/runtime documentation, author-maintained GitHub repositories, and primary teaching research. No external course exercises or solutions were copied. The following is a design synthesis for this learner, not a claim that one course is universally best.

Resource or technique Why it belongs here Concrete course change
Brown experimental Rust Book and its linked ownership research Makes misconceptions observable through prediction and visual ownership reasoning Session 02 asks for an owner/borrow/last-use trace before compiler feedback; every session starts with a diagnostic prediction
Google Comprehensive Rust A structured path for programmers with existing experience Keep familiar programming basics short; spend practice time on Rust contracts, memory, concurrency, and failure behavior
Mainmatter 100 Exercises, Rustlings Short exercises provide optional syntax and compiler-feedback practice Each workshop uses an original reproduce → change → transfer ladder; external drills are optional and linked rather than reproduced
Tokio select, blocking tasks, shutdown Resource and cancellation semantics matter directly to AI serving Sessions 07–10 require lifecycle traces, partial-message cancellation tests, and explicit shutdown accounting
Proptest, Loom, cargo-fuzz Different failure classes need different testing methods Optional generated retrieval properties, tiny concurrency models, and ingestion fuzzing; each tool's scope and setup limits are stated
Rust Performance Book and Criterion Optimization needs representative experiments and equivalent work Sessions 13–18 require correctness oracles, input-size sweeps, conversion-inclusive measurements, and rejection criteria
Rayon, SIMD status, rustc PGO, Miri Parallelism, compiler tuning, and unsafe code each have separate contracts Worker-count sweeps, reduction tolerances, scalar fallback, held-out PGO workloads, and safety arguments
wrk2, HdrHistogram Completed-request latency can conceal overload and generator effects Session 19 records offered/admitted/completed/rejected/timeout counts, generator lag, and queue-inclusive latency
PyO3, rust-numpy, argmin, SciPy gradient checking Native kernels need valid boundary semantics and numerical evidence Sessions 11/20 measure call and copy costs; Session 22 checks gradients and compares time to a fixed quality target

Quality audit and boundaries

Earlier notes provided topic explanations and broad lab specifications, but not a consistent path for diagnosing misconceptions or deciding what counts as a satisfactory submission. Every session now has measurable goals, a prediction, worked reasoning, three staged tasks, a collapsible hint, review evidence, and targeted primary reading. Earlier sessions are deliberately retrieved again in later work.

The original three persisted checkpoints per session retain their order and keys. New predictions are practice prompts, not automatically graded questions. Progress remains self-assessed. No added session hours are implied: use the workshop to guide the existing lab time, rather than treating all linked resources as mandatory reading.

Library documentation is live. Pin crate versions in actual lab implementations and use matching documentation; PyO3 main may be ahead of a released crate. Portable SIMD is optional nightly work according to the status checked on the research date. Tool availability differs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Proposed lab experiments have no promised speedup. Rust examples and lab specifications must still be compiled and exercised in the learner's Rust environment; website build checks do not validate Rust execution.

Learning-design revision — 18 October 2026

The earlier whole-project blank-file requirement was broader than the evidence supports. The course now combines worked examples, repair/completion, selected short core probes, AI-assisted engineering, and evidence-based review. This is a design synthesis for an experienced Python AI engineer learning Rust, not a proven optimal method or schedule.

Evidence Design implication and limit
Shen and Tamkin, 2026 AI can compromise immediate comprehension when learning an unfamiliar async library; this does not establish that every task must be written unaided or measure long-term retention.
Kazemitabaar et al., CHI 2023 AI improved novice code authoring without detected harm to manual modification; one-week post-test differences were not significant. Young participants and older tools limit applicability here.
Hou et al., 2023 Parsons scaffolding benefited some learners during practice, supporting an intermediate repair/completion step instead of universal unsupported writing.
Cognitive engagement techniques The second experiment found no significant post-test performance difference; interventions could add substantial time. Guided questions are not a proven universally superior method. Avoid compulsory repetitive questions.
Cui et al., 2025 Pooled enterprise trials found more completed tasks. Productivity does not establish learning or retention.
Crichton et al., OOPSLA 2023 Ownership models and visual explanations improved concept-inventory scores; use owner/borrow traces alongside compiler feedback.
METR, February 2026 Changing tools and selection effects limit extrapolating early-2025 productivity results to current workflows.

The routes in LEARNING_PATHS.md apply these choices. No direct comparison identified in this review proves a blank file plus compiler/API docs is best for experienced AI engineers learning Rust with 2026 tools. Record AI assistance separately from competence; assess explain, decide/build, verify/debug, and adapt. Revisit the design using actual learner errors, transfer, and later recall. The research supports neither a blanket ban on AI nor treating generated passing code as proof of understanding.
documents.assessment:
Assessment and study method

How to study each module

  1. Predict a small example's output or compiler error before running it.
  2. Read the lecture and only the assigned external topic.
  3. Use the session learning route: repair an example, attempt its focused probe, then implement the lab with AI collaboration and explicit verification.
  4. Test normal, boundary, and failure cases.
  5. Explain who owns the important data and what happens on failure.
  6. Record one mistake, its cause, and the evidence that corrected your understanding.

Use AI assistance as a tutor: request hints, compiler-error explanations, and review. Before accepting generated code, explain its ownership and failure behavior yourself. A passing test suite with an unexplained design does not pass the mastery gate.

Initial diagnostic — 30 minutes

Without Rust, sketch answers using your existing experience:

  • A FastAPI handler launches a background task; what should happen if its client disconnects?
  • Ten thousand requests arrive but inference handles four concurrently. Where does the remainder live?
  • A tool call times out after changing external state. Is retry safe?
  • A dataset is larger than RAM. Which pipeline stages might accidentally retain it?
  • A Python function spends most time in an optimized native library. What evidence would justify replacing it?

These questions identify systems topics to revisit; unfamiliar Rust syntax is not a diagnostic failure.

Rubric for each lab: 100 points

Area Points Evidence
Correct behavior 35 Stated contract and edge cases pass
Ownership and API design 20 Intentional moves, borrows, copies, and clear boundaries
Failure and resource handling 20 Errors propagate; work/memory/capacity bounds are explained
Verification 15 Reproducible tests with meaningful failure scenarios
Explanation 10 Concise design note and oral walkthrough

Pass at 80 with no unresolved core contract violation. For early labs, resource handling means input and error policy rather than advanced async machinery. A benchmark improvement cannot compensate for incorrect results.

Checkpoint answer guide

Read after attempting the lecture questions. These are reasoning anchors, not scripts to memorize.

Module Essential explanation
01 Absence is different from measured zero; slices borrow; final expressions determine block values.
02 Moving String transfers ownership without requiring a deep heap copy; borrowing shares access under restrictions; cloning creates independent owned data at a cost.
03 Enums constrain representable shapes, while transition legality and side-effect policy require additional logic. A timeout is ambiguous about remote completion.
04 Lifetimes describe reference validity relationships; they cannot extend a local allocation. Borrowed results depend on input storage.
05 Incremental reads are insufficient if a line, error list, or deduplication set grows without bound. UTF-8 boundaries and model-token boundaries differ.
06 Arc provides shared ownership, not unsynchronized mutation. Worker-local aggregation can reduce contention. Producer/consumer rate mismatch requires policy.
07 Futures need polling. Spawned tasks need suitable captures, and join errors differ from operation errors. Dropping a JoinHandle does not reliably cancel its task.
08 Active concurrency, queued work, and ingress body allocation are separate limits. Cancellation is not transaction rollback.
09 Validate before scarce work; reuse clients; distinguish process liveness from service readiness. HTTP errors require a stable mapping.
10 HTTP status is committed once sent; capacity spans the body lifetime. Network chunks need not align with application events.
11 Boundary conversions and batch size may dominate native execution. Equivalent behavior is a prerequisite for benchmarking.
12 Rust enforces certain memory/type properties, not availability or application correctness. Adoption should follow workload evidence and maintenance costs.

Reference-code review

Exercise 01 converts to floating point before summing. This avoids integer overflow but accepts approximation. Exercise 02 returns a trimmed slice into the input; its pointer test checks that it is borrowed. Exercise 03 checks configuration validity before request comparison. The tests express these contracts, but passing them does not prove every possible implementation correct; review the implementation too.

Spaced review

Revisit ownership one day after module 02, one week later, and before module 07. Revisit one earlier bug or focused function with a changed input or constraint. At the end of each module, explain a compiler error you once misunderstood without looking at notes.

Tutor prompts

Teach module 02 from this course. Ask me to predict ownership behavior before explaining it. Give hints in stages and do not reveal the solution immediately.

Review my Lab D implementation against its stated acceptance criteria. Trace task and permit lifetimes on timeout, cancellation, and shutdown. Separate demonstrated problems from assumptions.

Assess my capstone using the course rubric. Ask me to defend the Python–Rust boundary using correctness and benchmark evidence.

Advanced checkpoint anchors

For sessions 13–22, use the same 100-point rubric and require a completed performance report. There is no required speedup percentage. Incorrect results, unbounded resource growth, or unsupported portability claims fail the contract even if the fastest measured case improves.

Session What a strong explanation establishes
13 Bottleneck evidence, timed boundaries, Amdahl assumptions, and measurement uncertainty.
14 Owner lifetimes, copies at queue boundaries, capacity retention, and outlier behavior.
15 Hot-field access, cache-sized versus larger workloads, bandwidth estimates, and false sharing versus true contention.
16 Scheduling overhead, task granularity, pool interactions, and exact top-k merge reasoning.
17 Precision/error contract, feature checks, safe tail handling, and stable fallback.
18 A deterministic total ordering, worst-retained heap root, k-dependent costs, and quality disclosure for approximation.
19 Queue/batch wait, fixed offered load, all outcomes, and deadline/resource recovery.
20 Storage ownership, layout/dtype policy, interpreter constraints, and the complete Python-call baseline.
21 Held-out workload results, build/deployment assumptions, and proof obligations not established by tests alone.
22 Equal objective scaling and stopping targets, gradient verification, convergence failures, and scheduling-independent randomness.
# Workshop review protocol

Use the Practice studio attached to the current session before marking it complete. Submit: (1) the exact contract and assumptions, (2) code or a focused diff, (3) commands, environment and relevant outputs, (4) edge/failure tests, and (5) one tradeoff or unresolved limitation. For performance work, also attach PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md with equivalent-work comparisons and correctness evidence. A faster incorrect result does not pass.

Teacher mode uses a worked example and targeted questions to diagnose the current misconception. Teammate mode can help generate and integrate code, while reserving the specified short Core probe for focused learner practice. Reviewer mode checks the declared contract first, reports concrete findings with evidence, and asks for a correction plus a new regression case where appropriate. Predictions are formative practice; the existing three saved checkpoints remain the durable reflection record.

Use three review outcomes: Ready (contract and evidence satisfied), Revise (specific correctness or evidence gap), and Stretch (optional improvement beyond the contract). Do not gate completion on an arbitrary speedup. At the next study block, explain one previous mistake without notes; revisit it about a week later. When a resource disagrees with your implementation, check versions and reduce the disagreement to a small reproducible example.

AI collaboration policy

Use LEARNING_PATHS.md and MASTERY.md for the current learning and review policy. AI-assisted implementations can reach Independent when you can explain, verify, debug, and adapt them. No whole-project blank-file requirement applies. Assess a short unaided Core probe only where the session route specifies one; other probes assess reasoning. Record assistance separately from demonstrated mastery.
documents.capstone:
Capstone: a bounded AI service gateway

Problem and scope

An inference endpoint is shared by multiple callers. Unrestricted concurrency creates unpredictable queues and resource consumption. Build a local gateway that validates requests, controls admission, forwards streamed responses, and explains failures through telemetry.

Use synthetic requests and a deterministic mock upstream. Connecting to an existing local inference server is optional and requires adapting its actual request/stream protocol. The deliverable is a learning prototype, not a production certification.

Architecture

Client
  -> HTTP validation and request ID
  -> bounded admission queue with absolute deadline
  -> limited active upstream requests
  -> reusable HTTP client -> mock or local inference server
  <- streamed bytes with body-lifetime capacity ownership
  -> structured completion/failure telemetry

Every queue must have a capacity and every task an owner responsible for shutdown. Preserve one end-to-end deadline across queueing and upstream work. Do not hold a global state lock over network I/O.

Milestones

  1. Contract: copy Lab E's local API into a README; define validation and error mapping. Add fixture requests and expected wire responses.
  2. Core service: route validation, configuration, request IDs, mock upstream, and a shared outbound client. Keep parsing separate from execution policy.
  3. Capacity: bounded queue, active cap, queue expiry, overload rejection, and capacity counters. Demonstrate the limits using controlled barriers.
  4. Streaming: incremental forwarding, fragmented chunks, downstream disconnect, and mid-stream failure. Keep capacity occupied until the body finishes or drops.
  5. Lifecycle: stop admission and drain active work within a configurable grace period. Define the fate of queued and unfinished jobs.
  6. Evidence: correctness suite, repeatable load script, results table, and a two-page architecture decision record.

Required failure demonstrations

Scenario Required observation
Invalid request No upstream request is started
Queue at capacity New request rejected according to API contract
Deadline expires in queue Job never begins upstream work
Upstream stalls before headers Deadline error and recovered capacity
Upstream fails mid-body Stream terminates; final telemetry records failure
Client disconnects Local work/resources released; upstream cancellation limitations documented
Shutdown during a stream No new admission; drain/termination follows configured policy
Worker/task fails Failure visible; service can accept later requests

Load experiment

Use fixed upstream response size/delay, a stated load-generation model, and fixed machine configuration. Test below capacity, near capacity, and sustained overload. Run at least five repetitions per case and retain raw results.

Report offered, admitted, rejected, successful, failed, cancelled, and unfinished counts. Define denominator and timing boundaries. Report throughput, success latency p50/p95, time to first content, queue wait, and peak process memory. Treat rejected/failed work explicitly rather than hiding it from a latency chart. Compare versions only under identical workloads.

No speedup target is required. A credible explanation of the bottleneck is more valuable than a misleading percentage. If comparing FastAPI and Rust, use the same upstream, concurrency policy, streaming behavior, and client workload.

Submission checklist

  • A clean checkout can be set up from documented commands.
  • Tests run without paid APIs, GPU availability, or client data.
  • Configuration, dependency versions, and application lockfile are recorded.
  • Each acceptance scenario has a test or reproducible demonstration.
  • Telemetry distinguishes HTTP response start from stream completion.
  • Decision record covers why Rust, why these boundaries, costs, alternatives, and remaining risks.
  • A five-minute demo follows one request through validation, queue, upstream, and teardown.

Review questions

Where can memory still grow? Who owns the request body, task, permit, and response stream? What remains running after the caller leaves? Which errors can be retried safely? Which facts are guaranteed by types, by tests, or only by assumptions? Which component would you keep in Python, and why?
documents.workbook:
Lab workbook

All data is synthetic. A lab submission includes code, tests, a command to reproduce results, and a short design note. Only foundation exercises 01–03 have supplied starter/reference implementations; Labs A–F are implementation assignments guided by these contracts.

Foundation exercises — modules 01–03

Work in practice/src/lib.rs. Run one named exercise suite at a time. The reference implementation is in practice/src/solutions.rs.

Exercise 01: latency summary

Implement mean_latency(values: &[u64]) -> Option<f64>.

  • Empty input returns None.
  • Values are nonnegative milliseconds; nonempty input returns an approximate arithmetic mean.
  • Do not overflow a u64 sum for large inputs.
  • Do not mutate or copy the input into a new collection.

Examples: [] -> None; [100, 200, 300] -> Some(200.0); [0] -> Some(0.0).

Stretch: implement p95 with an explicitly chosen definition. For nearest-rank p95 on a nonempty sorted sample of n values, use rank ceil(0.95*n) with one-based indexing. Explain why a streaming exact percentile has different memory requirements from a streaming mean.

Exercise 02: borrowed prompt selection

Implement first_nonempty(values: &[String]) -> Option<&str>.

  • Inspect entries in order and trim surrounding whitespace using Rust's str::trim semantics.
  • Return a borrowed view of the first nonempty result.
  • Return None when all entries are blank or input is empty.
  • Do not allocate an output string or mutate the source.

Example: [" ", " retrieve ", "answer"] -> Some("retrieve").

Stretch: draw owner/reference lifetimes and show an intentionally noncompiling attempt to return a reference into a local String.

Exercise 03: validated token budget

Implement validate_budget(requested: u64, limit: u64) -> Result<(), BudgetError>.

  • A zero limit always yields ZeroLimit, even when requested is zero.
  • Otherwise requested above limit yields Exceeded { requested, limit }.
  • Equality and zero requested with positive limit are valid.

Stretch: introduce a TokenBudget type with a private field and a validating constructor. Explain whether allowing zero requested is suitable for your eventual HTTP contract; different layers can intentionally use different constraints.

Lab A — AI telemetry analyzer

Modules: 02–03. Budget: four to six hours, included in module allocations.

Start with this simplified CSV-like format, avoiding a serialization dependency initially:

request_id,latency_ms,status
r1,120,ok
r2,800,timeout
r3,240,ok
r4,invalid,ok

This format has no quoting or embedded commas; it is not a general CSV parser. Later use an established parser if broadening the format.

Build: a CLI that skips the exact header, classifies rows, and prints total valid requests, success count, timeout count, invalid count, and mean latency of successful requests. Unknown statuses and missing/extra fields are invalid. IDs must be nonempty. Reject negative or nonnumeric latency.

Expected report for the fixture: valid=3, success=2, timeout=1, invalid=1, successful mean=180 ms. Empty valid input yields no mean, not zero.

Acceptance: no panic on malformed rows; correct boundary handling; typed status enum; parsing separate from aggregation; tests for header-only input and malformed rows. Record why the parser borrows or owns each field.

Hint: start with a pure parse_row(&str) function and an enum for status. Handle row errors at the caller so one bad row does not end the run.

Lab B — Retrieval core without document copies

Module: 04. Budget: four hours.

Create three documents:

ID Text
a rust agent gateway
b python model training
c rust model serving

Scoring contract: split query and text on ASCII whitespace, lowercase ASCII letters, deduplicate tokens within each side, and score by the number of distinct overlapping tokens. Punctuation remains part of a token. For query rust model, scores are a=1, b=1, c=2. Return top two as c then a; break score ties by ascending ID. Empty query returns an empty result. k=0 returns empty. k above collection size returns all candidates for a nonempty query, including zero-score candidates. Reject duplicate document IDs at construction.

Build: Document, Scorer, and a ranking function returning document references and scores. Avoid cloning document text. Explain allocation in normalization and score metadata.

Acceptance: deterministic ties; explicit lifetime relationship; tests for repeated query terms, case normalization, empty collections, and zero matches. If generalizing to floating-point scorers, define a nonfinite-score policy before sorting.

Hint: first write a plain loop; optimize only after verifying the contract. This scorer is a teaching baseline, not semantic retrieval.

Lab C — Bounded JSONL ingestion

Modules: 05–06. Budget: six to eight hours.

Input schema:

{"id":"doc-001","text":"A synthetic drilling report."}

Each nonblank line must be a JSON object with nonempty trimmed id and text. Unknown fields are allowed and ignored. Blank lines count as skipped. Duplicates are allowed in the base lab so no global ID set is needed. Report duplicate policy explicitly.

Build: incremental reader, parser, validator, and character-boundary chunker. Default maximum line size is 64 KiB of bytes excluding newline; default chunks contain at most 256 Unicode scalar values, without overlap. This is character chunking, not model tokenization. Keep total counters and only the first ten error summaries, including line number and category. Do not retain full text in errors.

Acceptance: output chunks reconstruct the trimmed text exactly; valid UTF-8 is preserved; malformed JSON does not halt later records; oversized lines are discarded up to the next newline without unbounded buffering. Reject invalid UTF-8 with a clear policy. Test a last line without newline, CRLF, giant records, and Unicode.

Measurement: generate increasing input sizes and verify that retained application data does not grow with total file length. Report the distinction between application buffering and OS/file-cache behavior.

Extension: add a fixed worker pool and bounded batches. Show equivalent output summaries, propagated worker failures, and an explicit ordering policy. Avoid unlimited per-record task creation.

Hint: a size check after an unbounded line read is too late to enforce a hard buffer bound.

Lab D — Bounded asynchronous tool executor

Modules: 07–08. Budget: eight hours across the two modules.

Represent synthetic jobs as ID, delay, outcome, and absolute deadline. Outcomes are success, retryable error, and permanent error. No real network calls are needed.

Build in order: serial executor; bounded concurrent execution; bounded queue; queue-aware deadlines; cancellation; shutdown. Configure four active jobs and eight queued jobs. A full queue rejects immediately. Use completion-order output and preserve IDs. Maximum active work must remain four.

Retry contract: at most two attempts total for explicitly retryable synthetic jobs, with a fixed testable backoff and sufficient remaining deadline. Permanent failures never retry. These mocks have no side effects; adding real tools requires a separate idempotency policy.

Acceptance scenarios:

  1. With controlled job start barriers, four active and eight queued jobs are accepted; the next is rejected.
  2. An expired queued job never invokes the worker.
  3. A never-finishing job reaches its deadline and releases capacity.
  4. Caller cancellation does not leave detached work running indefinitely.
  5. Retry counts and deadline consumption match the contract.
  6. Shutdown rejects new work, reports discarded queued jobs, and drains active work for a defined grace period.

Use barriers/notifications and controlled time instead of fragile short real-time sleeps. Track active count and maximum observed count. Return success, failure, rejected, or cancelled for every submitted ID.

Hint: bound admission before creating work that can accumulate. A semaphore around an unlimited number of spawned tasks only limits one part of the resource problem.

Lab E — Inference gateway

Modules: 09–10. Budget: eight hours.

Use a local mock upstream first. Implement a small course API:

{"model":"mock-model","prompt":"Summarize this synthetic report","max_output_tokens":128}

Contract: POST /generate; JSON body at most 64 KiB; nonempty trimmed prompt; model from a configured allowlist; output budget 1–4096. Return a byte stream from a documented mock protocol. This does not claim full OpenAI API or MCP compatibility.

Build: reusable HTTP client, explicit error responses, bounded admission, queue-aware deadline, request IDs, streaming forwarding, and shutdown. Upstream URL comes from configuration, not an arbitrary caller-supplied URL. Keep permits alive for the complete streamed body.

Acceptance: validation, overload, pre-header timeout, upstream rejection, partial-body failure, fragmented event boundaries, downstream disconnect, and shutdown are tested. For mid-body failure, terminate and record a correlated stream error; never pretend to replace the already-sent HTTP status. Disable retries after forwarding bytes.

Observability: report queue wait, time to upstream headers, time to first forwarded content, total stream duration, final outcome, and active count. Do not log prompt text by default.

Hint: do not materialize the entire upstream response before returning it. Test that first content reaches the client while the upstream is still producing later content.

Lab F — Python extension with honest measurement

Module: 11. Budget: four to six hours.

Operation: normalize a list of IDs. Strip only ASCII spaces from each end, change ASCII A–Z to a–z, preserve internal characters, order, duplicates, and empty strings. Non-ASCII characters remain unchanged. Input elements must be Python strings; reject other values with an exception.

Build: pure Rust core, PyO3 wrapper, and Maturin packaging in a separate package/virtual environment. Implement an identical Python baseline. Use the current official guide for the installed API version.

Acceptance: parity on empty batches, ASCII whitespace distinctions, Unicode, duplicate and invalid inputs; installable wheel; no panic exposed as expected input handling.

Benchmark: batches of 1, 100, 10,000, and 100,000 fixed synthetic IDs. Use warm-ups and at least 20 repeated calls per case; report median and p95 with the percentile convention stated. Measure the complete Python call and pure Rust computation separately. Record whether conversion overhead changes the conclusion. A correct report showing no speedup passes.

Hint: Python's default strip() and Unicode lower() do not implement this deliberately narrow contract; use equivalent ASCII rules.

Session 13: Profiling, experimental design, and performance budgets

Lab G: a performance investigation

Generate seeded JSONL datasets with 10k, 100k, and 1m records, plus small and large text variants. Profile your core ingestion pipeline and rank three hypotheses by expected impact. Implement one change only. Report throughput, time per record, peak memory, allocation evidence when available, and correctness parity. Run at least five independent process repetitions; distinguish those repetitions from a benchmark framework's internal samples. Include exact commands, input seed, compiler, dependencies, build profile, and hardware. Acceptance requires a reproducible report even if the change is neutral or slower. Do not invent profiler counters that your tool cannot collect.

Sources

Rust Performance Book: profiling, Criterion guide, std::hint::black_box.

Session 14: Allocation control, borrowing, and buffer reuse

Lab H: an allocation-aware normalizer

Implement a batch normalizer with identical ASCII rules to core Lab F. Compare an allocating baseline, a borrowed/owned representation, and worker-local reusable buffers. Include already-normalized inputs, heavily modified inputs, Unicode, empty records, and a single huge outlier among small records. Verify byte-for-byte parity, report allocations/record when measurable, and measure retained memory after the outlier. Acceptance requires an explicit buffer-retention policy and no references into overwritten storage. A lower allocation count alone does not establish lower end-to-end latency.

Sources

Performance Book: heap allocations, Cow, Vec.

Session 15: Data layout, cache locality, and memory bandwidth

Lab I: candidate scoring layouts

Implement a reference dot-product scan over finite f32 embeddings, accumulating in f64, then compare an array-of-structs and flat row-major storage. Use dimensions 128, 768, and 1536 with data sizes below and above last-level cache where feasible. Preserve IDs, validate dimensions, and include malformed shape tests. Report elapsed time, estimated input bytes/second, and peak memory. Add metadata large enough to test whether separating hot fields matters. Acceptance requires an access-pattern explanation and correct ID mapping; the experiment may show no advantage for one layout.

Sources

Performance Book: types, Rust Reference: type layout, slice APIs.

Session 16: Parallel CPU pipelines with Rayon

Lab J: parallel exact scoring

Extend Lab I with a custom Rayon pool and partition-local top-k. Test 1, 2, 4, and more workers when hardware permits, both uniform and skewed batch sizes, and tiny versus large datasets. Use the exact tie contract from Lab L. Report speedup relative to the same optimized one-worker implementation, efficiency, memory, and result parity. Cap total work in flight. Acceptance includes a measured break-even batch size and a policy for Python/native pool interactions, not just a best-case chart.

Sources

Rayon API, Rayon repository, ThreadPoolBuilder.

Session 17: Vectorization, SIMD dispatch, and numeric correctness

Lab K: vectorized similarity kernel

Compare the scalar reference, an idiomatic stable loop, and one optional SIMD implementation. Test dimensions 1, 3, 7, 128, 769, and 1536, plus mismatched dimensions and the selected nonfinite-input policy. Measure small-call dispatch overhead separately from large-batch throughput. Verify fallback execution and record compiler/CPU features. Acceptance requires bounded error, correct tails, and a portable baseline; no minimum speedup or unsafe code is required.

Sources

std::arch, std::simd status, Rust Reference: target_feature.

Session 18: Exact top-k, indexing, and RAG retrieval efficiency

Lab L: retrieval selection shootout

Implement full sort as the oracle, a bounded heap, and an index-based partial-selection approach. Test n=1k/100k/1m where memory permits and k=1/10/100/n. Include ties, reverse input order, duplicate IDs, NaN/infinity rejection, empty input, and k=0. Differential tests must return identical IDs and order. Report score-computation time separately from selection and materialization. Acceptance requires an algorithmic argument, memory accounting, and a benchmark matrix rather than one favorable k.

Sources

BinaryHeap, slice selection and sorting, f32::total_cmp.

Session 19: Tail latency, batching, and queue optimization

Lab M: a latency budget for the gateway

Extend the core mock gateway with optional microbatching for a synthetic preprocessing operation. Compare no batching with bounded batch-size/wait combinations. Use fixed-seed mixed small/large requests and an open-loop arrival schedule. Report queue wait, time to first content, p50/p95/p99 completion latency, throughput, failure counts, and peak memory. Acceptance requires deadline expiry before execution, capacity recovery after cancellation, and an explicit tradeoff recommendation. Do not claim a p99 improvement without stating sample size and measurement boundaries.

Sources

Tokio tutorial, Tokio semaphore, Tokio shutdown.

Session 20: Python–Rust boundary optimization and zero-copy tradeoffs

Lab N: batched numerical scoring from Python

Expose the Lab I scoring operation through PyO3 using the current Rust NumPy bindings as an optional implementation route. Start with owned inputs if borrowing would obscure correctness. Define supported dtypes and layout; test contiguous, sliced/noncontiguous, empty, malformed-shape, and invalid-dtype inputs. Benchmark batches 1/32/1024/large with an equivalent NumPy baseline and controlled thread counts. Acceptance includes lifetime documentation, clean-environment installation, numerical tolerance tests, full-call measurements, and an explanation of any copy. No claim of universal zero-copy is allowed.

Sources

PyO3 performance guide, Rust NumPy bindings, Maturin guide.

Session 21: Code generation, build profiles, and justified unsafe boundaries

Lab O: an optimization change review

Choose a measured hot function from an earlier lab. Compare baseline release, one build-profile change, and one safe API/layout restructuring. Propose an unsafe variant only if useful; supplying a written rejection is acceptable. Report runtime, compile time, binary size, portability assumptions, correctness tests, and rollback criteria. Acceptance requires a reviewer-readable safety argument for any unsafe code and a held-out workload. Never disable required validation or change output semantics to manufacture a speedup.

Sources

Cargo profiles, rustc PGO, Rustonomicon, Miri.

Session 22: Numerical optimization engines and experiment throughput

Lab P: optimizer throughput capstone

Generate deterministic well-conditioned ridge problems and a synthetic bounded black-box objective for population evaluation. Implement the reference solver, one measured systems optimization, and a controlled parallel population evaluator. Verify gradients, termination, reproducible candidate values across worker counts, and objective parity. Compare with an equivalent Python/NumPy or established solver baseline, documenting algorithm and stopping-rule differences. Submit convergence plots, time-to-target distributions, evaluation counts, memory measurements, and a two-page decision record. Your implementation must report nonconvergence honestly. No paid service or proprietary client dataset is required.

Sources

argmin documentation, argmin source and examples, Rayon, ndarray.
documents.workshops:
Session workshops: predict, build, defend

Original course activities, researched 18 October 2026. Read each prediction before revealing the hint. These workshops supplement the existing lectures and lab contracts. They fit within the existing session budget; external courses are optional practice, not additional required courses.

For an eight-hour core session, budget roughly 20 minutes for retrieval of prior learning, 80 for explanation and examples, 240 for implementation, 80 for testing and review, and 60 for the checkpoint and corrections. For a ten-hour advanced session, add two hours for experiments and interpretation. Split this across several study blocks. Revisit one mistake in your next session and again a week later. These timings are a course design choice, not a claim about an experimentally optimal schedule.

Code below is illustrative unless explicitly described as a complete program. Compile fragments inside a suitable function or test. Rust execution is local; the website does not run code. Keep dependencies and toolchain versions in your lab report. Use stable Rust by default; advanced tools may require separate nightly or platform-specific setup.

01 — Make telemetry assumptions executable

Observable goals

  • Write a function accepting both borrowed arrays and vectors through a slice.
  • Specify empty-input behavior and units before implementing statistics.
  • Explain a compiler type error using the expected and actual types.

Predict and inspect

For latencies [0, 500, 501] and the rule latency > 500, predict the slow count and mean. Now predict the result for an empty input. Which answer represents missing observations without inventing a measurement?

Worked reasoning

The count is 1; the approximate mean is 1001.0 / 3.0. A function returning Option<f64> can distinguish None from Some(0.0). Converting each u64 before summation avoids integer-sum overflow, but does not provide exact arithmetic for all large integers. Write that limitation in your contract. In Python, an empty NumPy reduction may produce a warning or NaN; here the return type makes the choice visible to callers.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: implement mean, maximum, and threshold count; test the three-element input above.
  2. Change: accept a threshold argument and test equality at 500. Run the same functions on an array and a vector.
  3. Transfer: design a LatencyMs wrapper and explain which mistakes it prevents and which values still require validation.
Hint — start with the contract

Return early on an empty slice. Maximum naturally returns an Option too. A domain wrapper distinguishes milliseconds from token counts; it does not prove the sensor measured correctly.

Review evidence: function signatures, empty/singleton/boundary tests, and one compiler error you can now explain. Revisit this contract when measuring latency in Session 19.

Targeted reading: Rust Book: functions, especially expressions; Rustlings repository, variables and functions, for optional short drills.

02 — Trace owners before repairing code

Observable goals

  • Identify the owner and final use of each borrow in a short program.
  • Repair a borrow conflict without an unnecessary clone.
  • Distinguish UTF-8 byte length from a token or character count.

Predict and inspect

let mut prompt = String::from("  agent  ");
let view = prompt.trim();
prompt.clear();
println!("{view}");

Predict whether this compiles. Mark the allocation, the owner, and the last use of view before asking the compiler.

Worked reasoning

view refers into prompt and is used after clear, so mutation conflicts with the active shared borrow. Printing view before clearing removes that overlap. Creating an owned copy also works, but has a different allocation contract. A lifetime annotation cannot make the conflicting accesses safe. Use the compiler's span information to compare your predicted last use with the actual one.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: compile the failing fragment, then repair it by reordering uses.
  2. Change: make a queued job own the trimmed text; explain why an allocation is now intentional.
  3. Transfer: add Vietnamese text and an emoji to your chunker tests. Define boundaries with char_indices; do not equate character counts with model tokens.
Hint — draw two different designs

A temporary view can borrow existing storage. A job retained after its source is dropped must own its text or retain an appropriate owner. Those are different API requirements.

Review evidence: ownership diagram, failing diagnostic, two repairs with cost explanations, UTF-8 tests. Retrieve Session 01's slice contract from memory first.

Targeted reading: Rust Book: borrowing; Brown ownership chapter for visual explanations and diagnostic quizzes.

03 — Test domain invariants at construction

Observable goals

  • Represent agent execution alternatives without contradictory flags.
  • Propagate an expected error through Result rather than panicking.
  • Check a token-budget calculation without overflow.

Predict and inspect

A request has a context limit of 8,192, a prompt of 8,000, and reserves 256 output tokens. Is it valid? What if prompt plus reserve exceeds the integer type's range before comparison?

Worked reasoning

The total 8,256 exceeds the limit by 64. checked_add distinguishes arithmetic overflow from an ordinary over-budget result. Use a constructor returning a domain error so callers cannot accidentally construct a validated request through public fields. An enum such as Execution::Failed { reason } couples the failure state to its explanation. Result does not automatically enforce valid transitions; transition methods still need rules.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: implement validation for exact fit, one over, and arithmetic overflow.
  2. Change: distinguish invalid configuration from a valid request that exceeds a budget.
  3. Transfer: define allowed agent transitions and test that a finished execution cannot become running again without an explicit new attempt.
Hint — separate two decisions

First establish that arithmetic is representable. Then compare the representable total with the limit. Keep validation fields private if every value of the type must satisfy the invariant.

Review evidence: error variants, a transition table, tests for all three arithmetic boundaries. Explain why unwrap in a test has a different purpose from unwrap on untrusted service input.

Targeted reading: Rust Book: recoverable errors; Comprehensive Rust sections on enums, pattern matching, and error handling. Optional drills: 100 Exercises repository.

04 — Make retrieval ownership and ranking precise

Observable goals

  • Explain a returned reference's relationship to its input lifetime.
  • Implement a deterministic scalar similarity reference.
  • State a policy for dimension mismatch, zero norms, and non-finite values.

Predict and inspect

Would fn best<'a>(items: &'a [Document]) -> Option<&'a Document> keep documents alive after their owner is dropped? Does a lifetime annotation allocate or extend storage?

Worked reasoning

The annotation describes a relationship checked at compile time; it does not retain the owner. For a similarity calculation, zip alone silently stops at the shorter input. Check equal dimensions before accumulation. For equal scores, choose a stable document-ID tie rule so two valid implementations have comparable outputs. Decide whether zero vectors produce a domain error or a documented special score before optimizing.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: write scalar dot product and cosine reference functions with explicit validation.
  2. Change: return a borrowed winning document rather than cloning its content.
  3. Transfer: compare an iterator implementation and a loop on the same generated fixtures. Add an optional Proptest property: valid top-1 scores are no lower than any candidate score under the chosen ordering.
Hint — correctness before abstraction

Start with one concrete Document type and a loop. Generalize with a trait only after identifying which behavior actually varies. Keep the simple reference for later differential tests.

Review evidence: dimension/zero/non-finite/tie tests, ownership explanation, scalar oracle. Reuse this oracle in Sessions 15–18.

Targeted reading: Rust Book: lifetime syntax; Iterator documentation, including zip.

05 — Bound ingestion by bytes as well as records

Observable goals

  • Define an ingestion memory budget including the largest record.
  • Report line-level errors while following a documented stop/skip policy.
  • Test parser behavior on malformed and oversized input.

Predict and inspect

A JSONL queue holds at most 16 records. Is memory bounded if a single record may contain a 1 GB string? Does reading one line at a time itself enforce a line-size limit?

Worked reasoning

A count bound needs a size bound. Reading a full line into a reusable buffer can still grow that buffer to an oversized line before validation. For hostile input, use a bounded reading strategy that detects the limit while reading, then fail or drain according to policy. A zero-copy parsed view may also prevent reusing the buffer until consumers finish. Ownership, throughput, and retention must be designed together.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: ingest valid, blank, and malformed lines with line-numbered diagnostics.
  2. Change: enforce a byte limit during reading and test exactly-at-limit and one-byte-over cases.
  3. Transfer: simulate a slow downstream consumer; record queue depth, buffer capacity, and peak resident memory separately. Optional parser fuzzing follows the Rust Fuzz Book; check its toolchain/platform requirements first.
Hint — write the memory equation

Estimate queue capacity × maximum retained record bytes, plus parser buffers and in-flight work. This is a design budget, not an exact RSS prediction; allocator and runtime overhead remain.

Review evidence: limit enforcement test, error policy, memory-budget calculation, and reproducible input fixture. Recall Session 02 before choosing borrowed records.

Targeted reading: BufRead API, especially read_line and fill_buf; Serde JSON documentation.

06 — Prove work is accounted for

Observable goals

  • Separate shared ownership from synchronized mutation.
  • Account for accepted, completed, failed, and abandoned jobs.
  • Explain shutdown behavior when producers or consumers disappear.

Predict and inspect

Two threads each load an atomic counter, add one locally, and store the result. Can the final count be one even if every operation uses sequential consistency?

Worked reasoning

Both threads may load zero before either store. Strong ordering does not turn a multi-operation sequence into one indivisible update. An atomic read-modify-write such as fetch_add addresses this particular counter; a multi-field invariant may need a lock or another design. Likewise, Arc<T> shares ownership but does not make arbitrary T mutations safe. Prefer worker-local results merged at a clear boundary when possible.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: implement the bounded worker pool with one and several workers; compare results with the sequential oracle.
  2. Change: inject a worker failure and close a sender early. Ensure shutdown cannot wait forever for an impossible event.
  3. Transfer: model a tiny accounting primitive with Loom. Replace relevant primitives with Loom equivalents; limit the model to two threads and a few operations. A passing bounded model does not prove the entire service correct.
Hint — list every exit path

Define accepted = completed + failed + explicitly abandoned at shutdown. Join workers and propagate failures. Do not hold a global result lock while doing CPU work.

Review evidence: job-accounting assertions, sequential comparison, shutdown tests, and an ownership diagram. Revisit the Session 03 error model.

Targeted reading: Rust Book: shared-state concurrency; atomic ordering API.

07 — Separate waiting from CPU execution

Observable goals

  • Explain why creating a future does not execute it to completion.
  • Choose between async I/O and a bounded CPU execution path.
  • Observe task results and failures instead of detaching them accidentally.

Predict and inspect

An async handler performs a long scalar embedding computation without reaching an await point. Will unrelated timers on the same runtime worker necessarily remain responsive?

Worked reasoning

Cooperative async scheduling relies on yielding. An async declaration does not turn CPU work into nonblocking work. Measure a heartbeat task while running the workload. A blocking-task facility moves execution, but unrestricted submissions can simply move the resource problem to another queue. Establish a concurrency bound, and remember that already-running blocking work generally cannot be stopped by dropping its awaiting future.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: run concurrent deterministic delayed tool calls and gather every result.
  2. Change: add a CPU-heavy mock and compare heartbeat lag before and after moving it to a bounded execution path.
  3. Transfer: define separate limits for external I/O requests and CPU jobs. Test failure propagation and shutdown with pending jobs.
Hint — observe the executor

Log task start, first poll, completion, and join outcome. A returned JoinHandle should have an explicit owner responsible for observing or cancelling it.

Review evidence: task lifecycle trace, heartbeat measurement method, concurrency-bound test. Recall Session 06's distinction between ownership and synchronization.

Targeted reading: Tokio: async in depth; Tokio spawn_blocking.

08 — Treat cancellation as a protocol event

Observable goals

  • Carry one end-to-end deadline across queueing and attempts.
  • Explain cancellation safety for each operation raced in select!.
  • Prevent retries from duplicating non-idempotent effects.

Predict and inspect

A read operation consumes part of a message, then loses a select! race. If you recreate the read future, can you assume no bytes were consumed? What happens to an upstream tool invocation after your local timeout?

Worked reasoning

Dropping a future stops polling that future; it does not roll back previously performed work. Cancellation behavior depends on the specific operation. A framed protocol can retain partial bytes in an owned buffer across waits. A deadline should include queue delay: a 100 ms budget with 80 ms already queued leaves roughly 20 ms, not another fresh 100 ms per retry. Remote side effects require protocol-level idempotency or reconciliation.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: test a bounded queue with deadline expiry while waiting for admission.
  2. Change: cancel at several framing boundaries; verify the next message is not corrupted.
  3. Transfer: build a retry table for connection failure, timeout after submission, and explicit rejection. State maximum attempts and remaining-budget checks.
Hint — read operation-specific guarantees

Consult the cancellation-safety section of the exact API. Store protocol progress outside a disposable future when required. A timeout response alone cannot establish that a remote operation never ran.

Review evidence: deadline trace, cancellation test matrix, bounded retries and idempotency policy. First retrieve the lifecycle from Session 07.

Targeted reading: Tokio select cancellation safety; Tokio channels.

09 — Make HTTP boundaries testable

Observable goals

  • Separate transport validation from domain validation.
  • Map expected failures to consistent status codes and bodies.
  • Apply request-size and concurrency limits before expensive work.

Predict and inspect

How should malformed JSON, a well-formed over-budget request, and an overloaded gateway differ? If JSON extraction fails before your handler body, does the handler's error mapping run?

Worked reasoning

Extraction and domain execution are distinct stages. A consistent service contract may need explicit rejection handling at the extractor boundary. Validate cheap constraints before scheduling inference. Define responses for malformed input, invalid domain values, overload, and internal failures without leaking sensitive internals. Share immutable configuration or deliberately synchronized state rather than cloning a large mutable model per request.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: test the router in process with a deterministic mock backend.
  2. Change: add malformed JSON, missing fields, oversized bodies, and domain-invalid requests; check both status and response schema.
  3. Transfer: saturate admission and verify rejected requests never invoke the backend. Count accepted and rejected work separately.
Hint — test the real boundary

Calling a domain function cannot test extractor rejection or middleware limits. Exercise the router with request bodies and inspect its actual response.

Review evidence: HTTP contract table, router tests, and backend invocation counts. Reuse Session 03's validated request type and Session 08's deadline.

Targeted reading: Axum extractors, rejection handling and body limits; Axum examples repository, choose testing and error-handling examples matching your pinned version.

10 — Design streaming across arbitrary chunks

Observable goals

  • Distinguish transport chunks from complete application events.
  • Bound buffering for slow clients.
  • Demonstrate a shutdown sequence that accounts for active streams.

Predict and inspect

An SSE event contains an emoji. Can one network chunk end in the middle of its UTF-8 bytes? Can several events arrive in one chunk? What happens if the consumer stops reading?

Worked reasoning

Transport boundaries do not define event boundaries. A decoder must retain incomplete bytes and frames until it has a complete valid event. For output, backpressure and disconnect propagation should stop unnecessary production. A shutdown policy needs an admission stop, a grace period, and a defined action when work outlives that period. A final log line is not proof that all producers and consumers terminated.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: encode a known event stream and decode it with each possible single split point.
  2. Change: test multiple events per chunk, a truncated final frame, and a slow reader.
  3. Transfer: disconnect a client during generation, then trigger shutdown. Verify producer termination and bounded retained events without logging private prompts.
Hint — keep protocol state explicit

Use a byte buffer until decoding is valid; do not assume each chunk is independently valid text. Trace stream ID and lifecycle transitions, with a separate policy for incomplete final frames.

Review evidence: split-point tests, slow-consumer test, disconnect trace, and shutdown accounting. Retrieve Session 05's byte-bound argument.

Targeted reading: Axum SSE API; Tokio graceful shutdown; tracing documentation.

11 — Choose a Python boundary deliberately

Observable goals

  • Package a small extension with repeatable build instructions.
  • Translate domain errors into appropriate Python exceptions.
  • Measure call, conversion, compute, and return costs separately.

Predict and inspect

A Rust kernel takes 2 microseconds per item, but each Python call adds 10 microseconds of boundary work. What is the approximate single-item cost? What changes if one call processes 100 items and has the same fixed overhead?

Worked reasoning

The simplified costs are 12 microseconds for one item and 210 for a batch of 100, or 2.1 per item. This calculation assumes fixed overhead and unchanged compute cost; it is a hypothesis to test, not a benchmark result. Python attachment and safe access to Python objects are API- and version-dependent. Keep Python object access outside detached numerical work, and never assume releasing interpreter attachment makes shared mutable buffers safe.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: expose one validated scalar function and test it from Python.
  2. Change: add a batch function and compare equivalent outputs with the Python reference.
  3. Transfer: measure empty-call overhead, conversion-only cost, and end-to-end processing; include wheel build and import instructions for your platform.
Hint — hold the workload constant

Compare the same inputs and amount of useful work. A NumPy reference should use its intended vectorized path rather than an artificially slow Python loop.

Review evidence: Python tests, error mapping, pinned PyO3/maturin versions, and a cost breakdown. Revisit ownership before storing borrowed Python data.

Targeted reading: PyO3 performance guide; maturin user guide. Use documentation matching your pinned release; main may describe unreleased behavior.

12 — Defend an integrated AI gateway

Observable goals

  • Integrate request validation, admission, deadlines, and streaming.
  • Demonstrate predictable behavior during overload and shutdown.
  • Explain architectural tradeoffs using evidence from a reproducible mock.

Predict and inspect

The backend becomes slow while new requests continue arriving. Which resource reaches its bound first? Which metric would distinguish queue waiting from model execution?

Worked reasoning

Draw the request path: parse → validate → admit → queue → execute → stream → release. Assign an owner, a bound, a deadline rule, and an observable event to each stage. A shared permit retained until a stream ends bounds something different from one released after response headers. Decide which resource your permit represents. A deterministic mock makes overload, cancellation, and shutdown reproducible without a paid model API.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: finish the capstone's happy path with a fixed-seed mock backend.
  2. Change: inject slow execution, backend failure, client disconnect, and shutdown during work.
  3. Transfer: propose one production extension and identify what your mock cannot validate, such as real provider rate limits or model-specific tokenization.
Hint — review one lifecycle end to end

Pick a single cancelled request and follow every task, permit, queue item, and buffer it owns. Then repeat for successful completion.

Review evidence: architecture diagram, run instructions, failure matrix, representative traces, bounded-resource tests, and a short tradeoff memo. Explain one rejected design. Review Sessions 08–10 without opening your notes first.

Targeted reading: Tokio mini-redis repository for lifecycle design; Axum examples for framework-specific patterns. Do not treat an example server as a complete production specification.

13 — Make an optimization claim falsifiable

Observable goals

  • State a measurable performance hypothesis and correctness guard.
  • Separate microbenchmark evidence from end-to-end impact.
  • Record enough context to reproduce and challenge a claim.

Predict and inspect

A function accounts for 20% of baseline time and becomes twice as fast. Can the complete workload become twice as fast?

Worked reasoning

With the remaining 80% unchanged, normalized time is 0.8 + 0.2/2 = 0.9, giving about 1.11× overall speedup. This assumes the workload and other costs stay constant. A faster microbenchmark can have no meaningful system effect when I/O or queueing dominates. Profile a representative workload, change one variable, and compare multiple input sizes rather than selecting the most flattering case.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: establish a release-build baseline and record toolchain, target, CPU, dataset seed, and commands.
  2. Change: implement one change behind an equivalent interface; validate outputs before timing.
  3. Transfer: compare isolated-kernel and complete-pipeline results, including a case that does not improve. Report uncertainty and repeatability, not just the fastest run.
Hint — define a rejection condition

Before running, write what would make you abandon the optimization: incorrect output, a memory regression, unstable gains, or no relevant end-to-end improvement.

Review evidence: completed PERFORMANCE_REPORT, profiler observation, baseline/variant commands, raw measurements, and correctness comparison. Retrieve the gateway bottleneck map from Session 12.

Targeted reading: Rust Performance Book on profiling and benchmarking; Criterion input benchmarks. Use std::hint::black_box where appropriate; it is not a proof of realistic workload behavior.

14 — Trade allocations against retention

Observable goals

  • Identify allocation sites and distinguish length from retained capacity.
  • Use borrowed output only while its owner remains valid.
  • Evaluate reuse and Cow using a realistic input distribution.

Predict and inspect

A reusable buffer sees one huge document followed by thousands of tiny documents. Does clear() return its capacity to the allocator? Would shrinking on every item necessarily improve throughput?

Worked reasoning

Clearing removes contents while keeping capacity for reuse. This can reduce repeated allocations and also retain a large outlier allocation. A retention policy might cap reusable capacity or replace unusually large buffers after use; test the churn this creates. Cow can avoid owning output on an unchanged path, but changed text still needs owned storage. A borrowed view also ties output lifetime to its source.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: compare always-owned normalization with an unchanged-input borrowed path.
  2. Change: reuse a buffer and add an outlier-size policy. Track allocation counts/bytes with suitable tooling and RSS separately.
  3. Transfer: vary the fraction of changed documents and size distribution; measure throughput and retained memory, including the huge-then-small case.
Hint — two budgets, two measurements

Allocation traffic measures work over time; retained capacity measures storage kept alive. Neither alone establishes process memory usage.

Review evidence: ownership diagram, Unicode-equivalence tests, allocation evidence, and the chosen retention rule. Review Session 02's borrowed output and Session 05's memory budget.

Targeted reading: String capacity API; Cow API; Performance Book: heap allocations.

15 — Match layout to the access pattern

Observable goals

  • Explain the bytes read by a candidate-scoring loop.
  • Compare layouts while including conversion and metadata access.
  • Keep bounds and dimensional invariants explicit.

Predict and inspect

Each candidate contains a 768-element f32 embedding plus a large text payload. A scoring pass uses only embeddings and IDs. Which fields need to be touched, and what is the minimum embedding data volume for one million candidates?

Worked reasoning

The embedding payload alone is 1,000,000 × 768 × 4 bytes, about 3.072 GB in decimal units. This is a traffic model, not a measured bandwidth result: caches, repeated passes, and representation affect actual traffic. Separating embeddings from cold metadata can help a scan, but transposition or packing adds costs and may harm other operations. Keep a plain layout as the oracle.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: implement scoring over nested vectors and a flat row-major buffer with validated dimensions.
  2. Change: separate metadata and vary candidate count and dimension across working-set sizes.
  3. Transfer: include packing and top-k metadata lookup in an end-to-end benchmark. Estimate effective useful-byte throughput and explain its assumptions.
Hint — optimize the measured loop

Draw the indices accessed by one query. Array-of-structures versus structure-of-arrays is a workload decision; neither layout wins universally.

Review evidence: layout diagram, shape tests, memory-size accounting, kernel and conversion-inclusive results. Reuse Session 04's oracle and Session 13's experiment contract.

Targeted reading: Performance Book: type sizes; Rust Reference: type layout. Do not assume unspecified struct layout or use packed representations as a casual performance fix.

16 — Parallelize useful work, then measure scaling

Observable goals

  • Keep mutable state local to parallel work where possible.
  • Compare worker counts and task granularity against a scalar reference.
  • Describe numerical changes introduced by reduction order.

Predict and inspect

Can a parallel floating-point sum differ from a sequential sum without a data race? Why might doubling worker count make a memory-heavy scan slower?

Worked reasoning

Floating-point addition is not associative, so a different reduction tree can change rounding. Decide whether your contract requires exact ordering, a tolerance, or a higher-precision reference. Parallel speed depends on useful work per task, synchronization, available bandwidth, and competing thread pools. A Python caller, BLAS, and Rayon can each create workers; total runnable threads matter more than one library's setting.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: parallelize independent candidate scoring using a controlled Rayon pool.
  2. Change: sweep worker count and chunk size; compare small and large datasets.
  3. Transfer: compare a global-lock accumulator with local partial results merged afterward. Test result equivalence under the declared floating-point/tie policy.
Hint — benchmark the crossover

Include workloads small enough that parallel overhead dominates. Run one benchmark configuration at a time and record other active thread pools.

Review evidence: scaling curve, thread configuration, correctness tolerances, and a justified sequential fallback threshold if one is useful. Review Session 06's accounting and Session 15's traffic model.

Targeted reading: Rayon parallel iterators; ThreadPoolBuilder.

17 — Vectorization with an explicit portability contract

Observable goals

  • Inspect generated code before claiming vectorization.
  • Validate tails, alignment assumptions, and numerical differences.
  • Preserve a portable scalar path for unsupported machines.

Predict and inspect

A vector kernel handles eight f32 values per iteration. Which elements are processed when dimension is 10? Can a binary compiled for your local CPU be assumed safe to run on every deployment machine?

Worked reasoning

One vector-sized group covers indices 0–7; a tail must handle 8–9. Test lengths below, equal to, and above the vector width, plus zero length. Compiler auto-vectorization should be the first investigation. Explicit target instructions require a deployment or runtime-dispatch contract. Portable SIMD's std::simd remains experimental and nightly-only in the documentation checked for this course; it is an optional branch, not a stable-course prerequisite.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: compare a clean scalar loop with compiler-generated assembly under the chosen release profile.
  2. Change: try one vectorization-friendly restructuring and test awkward lengths against an f64 reference with declared tolerances.
  3. Transfer: if using architecture intrinsics, add feature detection and scalar fallback; document every unsafe precondition and test the fallback directly.
Hint — separate correctness from dispatch

Kernel tests should cover every length category. Dispatch tests should prove unsupported features choose a valid fallback. A benchmark on one CPU tests neither universal portability nor all unsafe inputs.

Review evidence: assembly excerpt, tail tests, tolerance report, and supported-target policy. Retrieve Sessions 13 and 15 before changing compiler flags.

Targeted reading: std::simd status; std::arch guidance.

18 — Optimize selection without changing retrieval semantics

Observable goals

  • Define total ordering, ties, and non-finite handling for scored IDs.
  • Compare full sort, bounded heap, and partition-based exact top-k.
  • Distinguish exact selection from approximate search quality.

Predict and inspect

For scores (A,0.9), (B,0.9), (C,0.2) and k=1, what should the output be? What about k=0, k>n, or a NaN score?

Worked reasoning

Define descending finite score followed by ascending ID, for example. Reject non-finite scores if that is your contract; total_cmp provides an ordering but does not decide the domain policy for you. Partition can identify a selected region without sorting it, so a final sort is needed if the API promises ordered output. Handle k=0 and k>=n before calculating a pivot index. This optimization preserves exact scores; ANN changes the search problem and needs recall evaluation.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: implement full-sort top-k as the oracle.
  2. Change: compare heap and partition approaches across n, k, ties, and already ordered input.
  3. Transfer: use generated fixtures to assert identical ordered IDs across all exact methods; separately describe an ANN recall@k experiment without presenting it as exact equivalence.
Hint — reuse the comparator everywhere

A heap may need an inverted comparator. Test which candidate sits at its root before trusting replacement logic.

Review evidence: ordering contract, differential tests, complete-result benchmarks including final sorting. Review Session 04's zero-vector policy and Session 17's score tolerance.

Targeted reading: slice selection API; BinaryHeap API.

19 — Measure overload, queueing, and tails honestly

Observable goals

  • Distinguish offered, admitted, completed, rejected, and timed-out requests.
  • Measure end-to-end latency including queue time.
  • Evaluate a batching policy under both light and heavy load.

Predict and inspect

A client sends the next request only after the previous reply. When the server stalls, does this client maintain the same offered arrival rate? Could low completed-request p99 hide many timeouts?

Worked reasoning

A response-paced generator reduces its offered rate during a stall. Use a scheduled-arrival workload when testing a fixed offered rate, and report generator lag so client saturation is visible. Define latency start at the scheduled or actual submission time explicitly. Track failures alongside successful latencies. Batch waiting can improve compute efficiency and consume the same deadline budget a request needs for useful execution.

Practice studio

  1. Reproduce: instrument queue wait, execution, and end-to-end duration in the mock gateway.
  2. Change: sweep offered load through saturation and report counts, throughput, p50/p95/p99, and queue depth.
  3. Transfer: compare fixed-size batching with a maximum-wait rule at low and high load. Include rejection and timeout rates in every comparison.
Hint — preserve the denominator

Record how many arrivals were scheduled and submitted, not just how many responses arrived. Include sample count and observation window; a percentile without these is difficult to interpret.

Review evidence: arrival method, generator-lag report, full outcome counts, latency distributions, and bounded-queue behavior. Reuse Sessions 08 and 12's lifecycle model.

Targeted reading: wrk2 repository for constant-throughput load generation and coordinated-omission discussion; HdrHistogram repository for histogram concepts. Check platform support before choosing a local tool.

20 — Validate numerical buffers at the language boundary

Observable goals

  • Specify dtype, shape, stride, ownership, and mutation policy.
